note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Upper respiratory infection.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Andrew Campbell is a 59-year-old male who presents today with an upper respiratory infection. The patient reports that he was doing some yard work in the last week or so and started to feel really tired and short of breath. He believes that he caught his first cold in the last few weeks and that it has gotten worse. He denies any history of seasonal allergies. The patient reports that he has been monitoring his blood pressure at home, but not as much on weekends. He denies any nausea or vomiting, diarrhea, or fevers. He does report some joint pain in his elbows and knees.

The patient endorses shortness of breath when lifting or carrying heavy bags of soil, but denies shortness of breath at rest. He has not had any coughing up of anything yet, but anticipates that this will occur soon.

The patient endorses fatigue from his depression, which he has been managing with barre classes.

The patient endorses elevated blood sugar levels while working during the week, but not on weekends.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: depression, type 2 diabetes, hypertension.

SOCIAL HISTORY

Patient reports that his wife got him into barre classes to help him relax.

MEDICATIONS

Metformin 1000 mg twice daily; lisinopril 20 mg daily.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Cardiovascular: Regularly strong heart sounds bilaterally without murmurs or gallops.
Respiratory: Scattered ronchi bilaterally on auscultation of lungs. Clear to auscultation with cough.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS OF EXAMINATIONS AND TESTS:
Chest x-ray obtained today is unremarkable without airspace disease or pneumonia.
Hemoglobin A1c was 8%.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
Upper respiratory infection.
- Medical Reasoning: This appears to be a viral syndrome based on the patient’s symptoms and examination findings today.
- Medical Treatment: We will send a COVID test today to rule out COVID-19 exposure. I have prescribed Robitussin for cough and ibuprofen for fever management until we know the results of the COVID test today. We will follow up in 4 months for repeat labs including hemoglobin A1c levels.
Depression.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient endorses fatigue from his depression which he has been managing with barre classes. We discussed this further today and I have recommended psychotherapy if he would like to pursue this option at a later date.
- Medical Treatment: We discussed continuing with current treatment options for depression today and I have recommended referral to psychotherapy if he would like to pursue this option at a later date.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
- Medical Reasoning: His hemoglobin A1c level is elevated at 8%. This warrants increasing his metformin dose to 1000 mg twice daily until we see repeat labs in 4 months’ time.
- Medical Treatment: Metformin increased to 1000 mg twice daily daily until repeat labs are obtained in 4 months’ time. We will follow up in 4 months for repeat labs including hemoglobin A1c levels as well as lipid panel testing due to elevated cholesterol levels noted previously on lab work today.
Hypertension.
- Medical Reasoning: His blood pressure is well controlled with lisinopril at a dose of 20 mg daily; however, we discussed additional testing due to elevated cholesterol levels noted previously on lab work today as well as increased risk factors for cardiovascular disease including age and family history of hypertension and stroke due to parental history of stroke at age old (father).
- Medical Treatment: Continue lisinopril at a dose of 20 mg daily until additional testing is completed. Order lipid panel testing today.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Annual exam.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Andrea Roberts is a 52-year-old female with a past medical history significant for rheumatoid arthritis, atrial fibrillation, and reflux who presents today for her annual exam. She has been doing well since her last visit. She has been walking and exercising as recommended and has been doing yoga, which has helped with her arthritis. She reports no joint pain or stiffness over the last year.

Regarding her methotrexate, she is still taking it once weekly and reports no issues with that.

She has been experiencing palpitations again, which started about a week ago. She notes that they start to flare up when she gets stressed. She has been trying meditation and running with her dog to relieve the stress but it hasn't really helped.

Regarding her atrial fibrillation, she had an event monitor placed last month which showed that she is in and out of atrial fibrillation. There was also a conversion pause noted.

She has noticed nasal congestion due to allergies but denies chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea or vomiting.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Reports well.
• Cardiovascular: Reports palpitations.
• Respiratory: Denies chest pain or dyspnea on exertion.
• Gastrointestinal: Denies nausea or vomiting.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. Slight 2/6 systolic ejection murmur appreciated in the right elbow area. No lower extremity edema noted.
Neurological: No focal deficits noted.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Autoimmune panel: Normal.
Event monitor: Positive for conversion pause.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Andrea Roberts is a 52-year-old female with a past medical history significant for rheumatoid arthritis, atrial fibrillation, and reflux who presents today for her annual exam. She has been doing well since her last visit. She has been walking and exercising as recommended and has been doing yoga, which has helped with her arthritis. She reports no joint pain or stiffness over the last year.
• Rheumatoid arthritis - Stable at this time; continue methotrexate 2.5 mg once weekly; may need to refer back to rheumatology if needed; refill methotrexate ordered today.
• Atrial fibrillation - In and out of sinus rhythm; refer to cardiology for cardiac ablation today; order referral to cardiology today.
• Reflux - Continue protonix 40 mg daily; continue dietary modifications avoiding coffee and spicy foods; order protonix refill today.

Emergency room follow-up.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Albert Powell is a 62-year-old male who presents today for emergency room follow-up. The patient was seen in the emergency room last week due to high blood sugar readings and he was concerned. He was admitted to the hospital, but denied that they saw a reason for his elevated blood sugar levels. He reports that his mother was hospitalized the last week and had a hip replacement. She is doing well now, but they have been grabbing meals at the cafeteria or picking up fast food on their way home. The patient reports that he has been eating poorly since then.

The patient denies chest pain or shortness of breath. He does report lightheadedness and dizziness, which he attributes to his elevated blood sugar levels.

The patient reports that he has been doing well with his diet during the week, but not as consistent on the weekends.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: Type 2 diabetes.
Psychiatric: Depression.
Transplant: Kidney transplant.

MEDICATIONS

Lantus insulin.

Cardiovascular: Slight 2/6 systolic ejection murmur heard at the left sternal border. No carotid bruits appreciated.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Albert Powell is a 62-year-old male who presents today for emergency room follow-up. The patient was seen in the emergency room last week due to high blood sugar readings and he was concerned. He was admitted to the hospital, but denied that they saw a reason for his elevated blood sugar levels. He reports that his mother was hospitalized the last week and had a hip replacement. She is doing well now, but they have been grabbing meals at the cafeteria or picking up fast food on their way home. The patient reports that he has been eating poorly since then.

Hyperglycemia.
- Medical Reasoning: His hemoglobin A1c is elevated at this time and we discussed this with him today in detail.
- Medical Treatment Plan: We will increase his Lantus insulin dose to 20 units at night and we will continue monitoring his glucose levels at home and adjust as needed based on results from home monitoring.
- Patient Education/ Counseling Plan: We discussed how important it is for him to continue monitoring his glucose levels at home and we discussed how important it is for him to eat healthy foods during the week as well as try to avoid fast food or grab-and-go meals on weekends when possible.
- Patient Agreements/Consents: The patient understands and agrees with all recommended medical treatment plans today.

note.objective_exam:

note.objective_results:

note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

The patient is a 43-year-old female who presents today for right arm pain. She reports that she was playing tennis when she hit the top of the net with her arm. She denies any swelling or numbness in her hand. She does report some pain when moving her wrist.

She has pain following hitting her arm on the net. On exam, she definitely has some tenderness over her distal radius, and she has pain when I stress especially her thumb and flex her thumb. I think what she has is basically just a strain and maybe a contusion to that muscle from hitting it. She certainly doesn't have a fracture.

Medical Reasoning: The x-ray of the patient's wrist was reviewed today and there are no fractures or abnormalities.
Medical Treatment: We will treat this conservatively with ice, anti-inflammatory, Motrin 800 mg three times a day with food. If it doesn't get better in the next week or so, we will follow up with you again.

Back pain.

She denies lower extremity numbness, tingling, and weakness. She endorses nasal congestion from seasonal allergies.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: Significant for hypertension.

SOCIAL HISTORY

Patient reports that she has been lifting more, probably around 3 times a week. She does not know if it was because she was doing deadlifts that day and then walked.

Constitutional: Denies fever, chills.
Respiratory: Endorses nasal congestion from seasonal allergies.
note.objective_exam:

Cardiovascular: Grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur stable to follow-up.
Musculoskeletal: Examination of the back reveals tenderness to palpation on the right lateral aspect of the lumbar spine. Pain with flexion and extension as well as negative straight leg raise.

Labs obtained today are all within normal limits.
note.assessment_and_plan:

Cheryl Ramirez is a 34-year-old female who presents today with back pain.
- Medical Reasoning: I think this is likely due to lumbar strain secondary to lifting something or exercising.

We will refer her to physical therapy for strengthening exercises of her back in order to continue working out and exercising. Continue lisinopril 10 mg daily as prescribed.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the importance of continuing to monitor her blood pressure at home and report any increases in readings.

- Order medications as discussed today.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Cradle cap.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Randy Gutierrez is a 9-month-old male who presents today for evaluation of cradle cap. The onset of his symptoms began last night with a runny nose and congestion. He also has been experiencing a low-grade fever, which was confirmed by rectal temperature today. He has been irritable and refusing to eat. His appetite has been inconsistent, and he has been going to bed late.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Fever.
• Respiratory: Runny nose, congestion, cough.
• Gastrointestinal: Decreased appetite.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Ears: Normal appearance.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Cradle cap.
- Medical Reasoning: This appears to be a viral infection at this time. Often sinus infections will start out as a virus and then will become bacterial infections if left alone and does not go away.
- Medical Treatment: I have prescribed Zarbee's for the stuffy nose. We will continue to monitor him for any worsening symptoms or development of a barky cough. If he develops a barky cough, we will prescribe his sister's medicine in half-teaspoon doses for 5 days. We discussed the use of honey with the patient today and advised against giving honey to babies under 1 year of age due to botulism spores.
- Patient Education: I advised the patient that cradle cap is just another term for dandruff and that we can treat it with head & shoulder's shampoo or selsun blue shampoo. We discussed using these shampoos twice per week, not every day but twice per week, as well as using baby oil or another product that will help get the scales out of his hair. I also advised him that cradle cap is not pH balanced for eyes so he should avoid getting it in his eyes when rinsing his hair.
- Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with the recommended medical treatment plan.

Acne.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Kayla Ward is a 15-year-old female who presents today for a new visit with her mother for acne located on the face, which started about two years ago and is present most every day. She has been using Persa-Gel and washing regularly, which is somewhat helpful. There are no associated symptoms including itching, bleeding, or pain.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: No additional past medical history.

SOCIAL HISTORY

She lives with her parents and sister. They have a dog, bird, and bunnies. She is in 7th grade and active in basketball, volleyball, and tap dancing.

FAMILY HISTORY

No significant family medical history.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Ears, Nose, Mouth: Multiple benign nevi on the trunk and extremities.
Skin: Scattered skin colored papules. Open and closed comedones. Erythmateous papules on the face, primarily on the forehead and with also some on the central cheeks and chin. The chest and back are relatively spared.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Kayla Ward is a 15-year-old female who presents today for a new visit with her mother for acne located on the face.

Mild to moderate acne, mostly comodonal with small inflammatory component.
- Medical Reasoning: Mild to moderate acne was noted today during examination of the patient's face. The patient has been using Persa-Gel as well as washing regularly which has been somewhat helpful but not enough to resolve her acne.
- Medical Treatment: I would like to start with a topical therapy first. Every morning she will wash her face with a mild cleanser then use a moisturizer labeled "noncomedogenic," with sunscreen SPF 30 or higher. This means it won't clog her pores. Now in the evening wash her face with the same cleanser and allow it to dry. Apply adapalene 0.1% cream in a thin layer to the areas she generally gets acne. I want her to start off using this a few nights per week and slowly work up to using it every night. If it is very expensive or not covered by insurance she can try different gel over-the-counter products such as Clean & Clear Persa-Gel in a thin layer or where she generally gets acne followed by noncomedogenic moisturizer.
- Patient Education: We discussed that atopic retinoid will cause some sensitivity so she will need to wear sunscreen when outside. It may also cause some dryness or irritation.
- Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with recommended medical treatment plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Breast reduction.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Julia Jones is a 25-year-old female with symptomatic macromastia, presenting for evaluation of breast reduction. The patient has attempted nonsurgical treatments, but the minimal relief. She is an ideal candidate for bilateral reduction mammoplasty.

The patient reports that she has been experiencing back pain since high school. She has been going to the chiropractor for a few years and reports that she does have bra strap indentations in her shoulders. She wears a g cup and mostly wears a 34E sports bra because it is more comfortable. She also reports that she experiences numbness and tingling in her hands and nipple pain. She also experiences rashes underneath her breasts due to sweating.

The patient denies any history of breast cancer in her family, but her mother was diagnosed at age 40. The patient states that she has not had any mammograms yet, but would like to start at age 30.

The patient denies tobacco use, alcohol use, or drug use.

She is currently studying psychology.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: Significant for migraine headaches.
Family: Mother with prior history of breast cancer at age 40.
SOCIAL HISTORY

Currently studying to be a psychologist.
Tobacco: No prior history.
Alcohol: Socially. One glass per week.
Drug: No prior history.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Breast: Inspection reveals asymmetrical breasts with severe ptosis bilaterally. There is no nipple retraction or discharge bilaterally. No breast tenderness, masses, or axillary lymphadenopathy palpable.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Julia Jones is a 25-year-old female with symptomatic macromastia, presenting for evaluation of breast reduction. The patient has attempted nonsurgical treatments, but the minimal relief. She is an ideal candidate for bilateral reduction mammoplasty.

Medical Reasoning:
The patient presents today for evaluation of symptomatic macromastia and wishes to undergo bilateral reduction mammoplasty. Her minimum required resection based on a BSA of 2.65 using the Schnur scale is 1792 grams which should be attainable given her extremely large breasts and measurements above. Given her extremely large breasts and the measurements above there is potential for using a nipple graft.
There are several risks associated with this procedure including infection, bleeding, hematoma formation, seroma formation, asymmetry of the breasts or nipples after surgery, scarring from the incision site(s), nipple graft failure or necrosis if used in this case as well as numbness or altered sensation in the nipples after surgery which can be permanent if nerve damage occurs during surgery.
The patient understands these risks and agrees to proceed with surgery today after reviewing all options and alternatives available to her today in detail with me today in clinic today.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Renal ultrasound.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Kelly Wood is a 41-year-old female who presents today for a renal ultrasound because of hematuria. She reports that she passed two stones last week and has had several episodes of bright red urine the color of cherry kool-aid over the past 6 weeks. She also reports that she has been constantly having to urinate and it hurts. Her pain was rated at an 8 on a scale of 0 to 10, with 0 being no pain and 10 being the worst pain imaginable. She denies any flank pain or tenderness in her lower back.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: Chronic urolithiasis.

SOCIAL HISTORY

Drinks more Mountain Dew than water.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Constitutional: Reports hematuria.
Genitourinary: Reports hematuria.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

PE Abdomen: No flank pain.
GU: Normal vaginal exam.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Urine dipstick today. Negative for leukocytes, nitrates, protein, ketone, bilirubin and glucose. Color yellow and clear, urobilinogen 0.2 EU/dL, pH 5.5 and specific gravity 1.020. There is a trace amount of blood in the urine and intact.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Primary diagnosis: Hematuria.
Secondary diagnosis: Chronic urolithiasis.
Medical Reasoning: The patient's renal ultrasound today revealed a left kidney stone non-obstructing but she does have one stone in her left kidney at this time. Her symptoms are likely due to her kidney stones as there was blood in her urine today but it has nearly subsided since passing two stones last week.
Medical Treatment Plan: I discussed with the patient that we do not need to perform any surgical intervention at this time due to the non-obstructing nature of her left kidney stone. We discussed dietary recommendations to avoid foods high in oxalate and animal protein as well as drinking more water daily to help prevent future kidney stones from forming. I provided her with a handout regarding dietary recommendations and foods to avoid.

The patient reports that she has been taking Lisinopril, Simvastatin 20 mg, Amlodipine, Levothyroxine, and Meclizine.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Cardiovascular: Endorsees chest pain.
Neurological: Endorses dizziness.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Constitutional elderly otherwise no acute distress.
Cardiovascular: S1 and S2 is preserved with a normal rate and regular rhythm. There is a 4/6 systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border with mild radiation to the carotids.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Diana Scott is a 100-year-old female who presents today for evaluation of a new worrisome heart murmur.
Probable one cardiac murmur.
- Medical Reasoning: Her s2 is relatively preserved which would be more consistent with moderate stenosis rather than severe stenosis as there are no signs of volume overload today. Some of her outside records do note diastolic dysfunction so it is possible she did have an echocardiogram at some point in the past.
- Patient Education: We discussed the possibility that this could be due to severe aortic stenosis but we will need to wait until after we review her echocardiogram results before making any recommendations regarding further testing or treatment options at this time.
- Medical Treatment: We will order an echocardiogram today to assess overall cardiac structure and function as well as valve view where there may be disease present. Depending on results as well as severity of her aortic stenosis we will need to consider an ischemic evaluation or further possibly perform an ECG monitor to assess overall burden of PVCS. At this point she appears asymptomatic so we will start with the echocardiogram only today.

Lightheadedness/dizziness - Meclizine prescribed for this symptom however it is possible that some of her lightheadedness/dizziness may be related to the Aortic Stenosis which we will evaluate further via Echocardiography performed in clinic today followed up with additional monitoring if needed based on findings from Echocardigraphy performed in clinic today followed up with additional monitoring if needed based on findings from Echocardigraphy performed in clinic later this week.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Breathing difficulty.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Charles Sullivan is a pleasant 45-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of breathing difficulty. He reports that he has noticed that his breathing is not what it used to be. He considers himself to be pretty healthy, but he admits that he has been moving out of the city for the past two years and bought a large plot of land. He enjoys hunting and has a refrigerator full of venison at home. He has been carrying out his normal activities without any issues until recently when he started experiencing shortness of breath. The onset of this symptom was gradual and he denies any acute onset. He also reports that his eyes water more than usual, which he attributes to allergies. He denies any nasal congestion or sneezing, but does report eye itchiness and eye watering. The patient denies any rash, angioedema, or throat swelling.

The patient reports that his symptoms are worse when he is near his cat or outside the house, but they are present in all three situations. The patient denies any travel history or exposure to new environments.

The patient reports that he experiences diarrhea after consuming large amounts of alcohol.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: Denies previous issues with allergies.

SOCIAL HISTORY

Patient enjoys hunting.
Patient has a dog that gets eye bugers.
Patient has experienced diarrhea after consuming large amounts of alcohol.
Patient denies any previous issues with allergies.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Constitutional: Reports shortness of breath.
Respiratory: Reports wheezing bilaterally in all lung fields.
Gastrointestinal: Reports diarrhea after consuming large amounts of alcohol.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Cardiovascular: Normal rate and rhythm without murmurs, gallops, or rubs auscultated bilaterally in the precordium. No murmurs heard in the carotids or neck vessels. No jugular venous distention noted.
Respiratory: Faint expiratory wheezing bilaterally in all lung fields.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Chest x-ray obtained today was unremarkable.
Pulmonary function test obtained today was unremarkable.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Charles Sullivan is a pleasant 45-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of breathing difficulty. His examination reveals faint expiratory wheezing bilaterally in all lung fields on auscultation. His chest x-ray and pulmonary function test were both normal today as well. We discussed this with him today and I have diagnosed him with newly diagnosed allergic asthma based on his history and examination findings today. I have prescribed him albuterol inhaler to use as needed for symptoms as well as Singulair 10 mg once daily to decrease the frequency of asthma attacks. We will proceed with allergy testing today to identify potential triggers for his asthma symptoms and discuss immunotherapy if necessary.

Bryan Brooks is a 39-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of back pain. The onset of his symptoms began yesterday when he was raking leaves in his yard. The patient reports that he does not normally do any physical activity. He states that his partner is also experiencing similar symptoms, but reports that his partner is more tolerant of pain than him.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Non-healing right foot ulcer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Gregory Hernandez is a 40-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of a non-healing right foot ulcer. The patient reports that he has had the ulcer for approximately 2 months. He states that it has recently become red and is draining. He was concerned about how it has healed. The patient believes that he may have gotten the ulcer from walking barefoot on the beach. He notes that he did see his primary care physician before coming in today, and they started him on antibiotics, but he did not pick them up from the pharmacy yet. He does not recall the name of the medication prescribed to him.

The patient reports that when he got the ulcer, there was no trauma to his foot or it just popped up all of a sudden.

The patient denies any specific pain, but does report some throbbing.

Regarding his diabetes, he takes his medication but does not check his sugars all the time. He is not sure what his last A1C was, but believes it was around 10.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Reports fever.
• Cardiovascular: Reports edema.
• Musculoskeletal: Reports pain in right foot.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

CV: Normal examination of the cardiovascular system.
Respiratory: Normal examination of the respiratory system.
GI: No abdominal tenderness or masses noted.
Musculoskeletal: Examination of the extremities reveals a 1 by 2 inch circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot proximal to the fifth metatarsophalangeal joint. There is some redness and drainage present. There is edema around it. There is fluid like you said that's coming out of it. I do not see any necrosis, odor or bony exposure.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-ray of right foot reveals no evidence of osteomyelitis.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Gregory Hernandez is a 40-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of a non-healing right foot ulcer.

Diabetic Foot Ulcer with possible infection.
Medical Reasoning:
The patient presents today with a non-healing right foot ulcer which we suspect may be due to diabetes mellitus as well as possible infection secondary to trauma from walking barefoot on sand at Dewey Beach in Delaware. His last A1C was around 10 which is definitely elevated and likely contributing to this non-healing process. We also suspect there may be an infection present secondary to drainage and redness present at this time as well as increased pressure over this area which can lead to further tissue breakdown and infection formation.
Medical Treatment:
The patient will be referred for an ABI ankle brachial index just to determine blood supply in his feet to see if we can actually heal this ulcer. We will also perform debridement here today just to take off some dead tissue and prescribe him clindamycin 400 mg twice daily for seven days to try and get rid of this infection which he currently does have as well as reduce some redness and drainage at this time. We discussed with him wearing a shoe while this is happening because if he wears regular shoes there will be pressure on this area which can irritate it further leading back into more tissue breakdown and possibly worsening infection formation so we discussed getting him a shoe where he can wear that for one month while we wait for healing to occur at that point we will reevaluate him again in two weeks at which point we may perform another debridement if needed at that time we will just take a look at how things are doing overall at that point I also advised him if anything happens between now until then please feel free to call us or go directly into urgent care or emergency room if needed.

Left ankle pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Stephanie Morales is a 36-year-old female today complaining of left ankle pain. She reports that she was walking to her car and slipped on some snow and ice. She fell and her left ankle turned underneath her. She was able to get up afterwards but it was very sore and started swelling and quite a bit of pain, making it hard to walk. She has tried ibuprofen, ice, and elevation for pain and swelling but it has helped a little bit.

She denies any bleeding or bruising. She denies any pain above her ankle, in her calf or lower leg.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Reports increased fatigue.
• Musculoskeletal: Reports left ankle pain.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neck: No bruits.
Respiratory: Lungs are clear bilaterally.
Cardiovascular: Grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur in the left lower sternal border unchanged from before.
Gastrointestinal: Normal bowel sounds. Otherwise normal examination of the abdomen.
Musculoskeletal: Examination of the left ankle reveals tenderness over the lateral malleolus as well as tenderness over the fifth metatarsal. There is some swelling, redness, and pain with valgus stressing of the ankle.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

The patient is a 36-year-old female who presents today for evaluation of left ankle pain.

Diagnosis:
- Left ankle sprain.
- Possible fracture of the fifth metatarsal.
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
- Hypertension.
- History of hypertension treated with Norvasc.
- History of diabetes mellitus treated with Metformin.
- History of hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine sodium tablets (Synthroid).
- History of hyperlipidemia treated with atorvastatin calcium (Lipitor).
- History of hyperuricemia treated with allopurinol (Zyloprim).
- History of hyperglycemia treated with metformin hydrochloride (Glumetza).
- History of hypokalemia treated with potassium chloride tablets (Klor-Con).
- History of hyperkalemia treated with potassium chloride tablets (Klor-Con).

Medical Reasoning:
The patient presents today for evaluation for left ankle pain. Her exam reveals tenderness over the lateral malleolus as well as tenderness over the fifth metatarsal. There is also some swelling, redness, and pain with valgus stressing of the ankle. Given these findings, I have diagnosed her with a left ankle sprain as well as possible fracture of the fifth metatarsal. Additionally, she has been seen previously for type 2 diabetes mellitus which is currently well controlled on Metformin. Her hemoglobin A1c last time I looked at Epic was about 6.8 which is really good so I think she's doing a great job managing that at home. We had talked about cutting off sweets and sugars as well as exercising more to help manage her blood sugar levels but she hasn't seen an ophthalmologist recently for her eye exam or checkup due to diabetes so we will schedule an appointment for that in the next couple weeks since she is due for one soon. Her blood pressure today looks pretty good at 120/70 mmHg but we had talked about watching that closely since she's been taking Norvasc for hypertension so we will order another hemoglobin A1c today to check baseline labs since it's been a while since we checked them last time as well as continue monitoring that if something changes we can get her into office sooner if needed. We will also go ahead and refill her Norvasc today since she needs refills.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Sore on the right foot.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Wayne Jenkins is a 43-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of a sore on his right foot. The patient purchased a new pair of shoes to travel with and the neuropathy he has been experiencing did not allow him to feel that they were too tight at first. He initially had a blister, which soon became a wound and he was seen by his PCP. He was placed on a round of antibiotics, which he completed yesterday. The wound looks about the same today. He denies any changes to the appearance of the wound, pain or drainage. Occasionally, he has issues with stability, which was a primary purpose of purchasing these shoes. He denies fever or chills.

The patient reports neuropathy.

MEDICATIONS

The patient is currently taking antibiotics.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Constitutional: Denies fever or chills.
Musculoskeletal: Reports issues with stability.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neurological: Normal sensation to light touch in the right foot.
Musculoskeletal: Examination of the right foot reveals a 1 x 2 inch circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot proximal to the right fifth metatarsophalangeal joint. There is some yellow slough present with minimal granulation tissue. There is no surrounding erythema or cellulitis and there is no evidence of fluid collection. There is no necrosis present. No bony exposure noted on vascular exam. Palpable bilateral femoral and popliteal pulses are present; no palpable DP or PT pulses but Doppler signs are present.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-ray of the right foot reveals no evidence of osteomyelitis.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Diabetic foot ulcer.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient presents today for evaluation of a diabetic foot ulcer on his right foot that has not been healing despite antibiotic treatment and debridement by his podiatrist last year.
- Medical Treatment: I have reviewed the results from today's x-ray which revealed no evidence of osteomyelitis which means there is no evidence of bone infection so that's really good news for him today. We will continue this until we see the wound shrinking and nice pink tissue is present and we will cover it with a dry sterile dressing once daily and apply collagenase ointment to it once daily as well. We will also continue wearing surgical shoes to take pressure off this area until we see improvement in his wound healing.
- Patient Education: I have explained all medical treatment options available to him today as well as recommended additional referrals if needed.
- Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with all medical treatment recommendations.

Regarding your diabetes, I have ordered an A1c in order to better assess how well you have been controlling your blood sugars long term as well as ordered a lipid panel in case we need to make any adjustments to your current medications based on these results.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Back pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Matthew Hill is a pleasant 44-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of back pain. The patient reports that his back pain has been worsening over the past month. He notes that he was previously told that he may have a fracture at the time of his fall 30 years ago, but denies any history of a fracture. The patient denies any history of trauma to the lumbar spine. He states that he has been unable to play football due to his back pain. He has tried NSAIDs in the past without relief. The patient reports that his symptoms are worse with sitting and standing and better with lying down.

The patient also reports left leg pain radiating from the hip into the calf and toes, which is described as an electrical tooth ache. He rates his current pain as 6 out of 10, but states that it can be worse up to 13 out of 10 when it is at its worst.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Reports fatigue.
• Musculoskeletal: Reports lower back pain, left leg pain radiating from hip into calf and toes.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

• Neurological: Sensory examination reveals decreased sensation in the left leg distally to the ankle and toes. Reflexes are brisk bilaterally in both lower extremities.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

MRI of the lumbar spine reveals a disk herniation at L4-5 vertebrae with nerve root impingement.
note.assessment_and_plan:

I also explained that this can be treated conservatively with epidural steroid injection today followed by physical therapy.
- Medical Treatment: We discussed medical treatment options today including epidural steroid injection today followed by physical therapy. We discussed conservative medical treatment options including epidural steroid injection today followed by physical therapy. We discussed medical treatment options today including epidural steroid injection today followed by physical therapy.
Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with recommended medical treatment plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Recent blood work.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Jacqueline Walker is a 68-year-old female who presents today for recent blood work. She reports that her primary care provider recently ordered blood work and informed her that she has hepatitis C. She is anxious about this news as she has been feeling fine.

The patient reports that she used to party a lot and even use IV drugs years ago, but she has been clean for over 15 years now. She currently smokes 1-2 cigarettes per day, previously 1 to 1.5 packs per day, and drinks approximately 1 beer per day, more on the weekends. She denies any known hepatitis C positive partners.

She reports that she used to drink a lot of alcohol more than she does now, but she drinks about a beer a day now. She also admits to smoking more than she used to, but has cut down significantly.

The patient denies any other medication conditions.

She reports that her only complaint is fatigue at the end of the day after working. She had a physical last week and there was nothing else noted at that time.

PAST HISTORY

Personal history: Intravenous drug use over 15 years ago; currently smoking 1-2 cigarettes per day, previously 1 to 1.5 packs per day; history of heavy alcohol use, but now drinks approximately 1 beer per day, more on the weekends.
Family history: Hypertension, diabetes, and depression.

SOCIAL HISTORY

The patient reports that she is a workaholic and tends to be busy with work lately.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

General: Appears in no distress. No jaundice on skin exam.
Respiratory: Lungs are clear bilaterally with no wheezes, rales or rhonchi.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm with a 2/6 systolic murmur appreciated.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

HCV antibody test was positive. Liver panel shows elevated AST at 39 but ALT, albumin and total bilirubin were all within normal limits.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Jacqueline Walker is a 68-year-old female who presents today for recent blood work. Her initial labs are consistent with hepatitis C so based on the information I just discussed with her today today we will confirm the diagnosis with some additional blood work that includes checking the HCV RNA and also the HCV genotype. We will also determine the severity of her liver disease by checking for fibrosis of the liver which we will do by ordering a special ultrasound. With this information I will be able to know how to proceed as far as treatment.
We will start all family members on same screening as you have had for you.

He reports that he has been using ice, Tylenol, and ibuprofen for his pain but they do not help. The pain is shooting, stabbing, sharp, and constant. It is worse with movement and better with rest. He denies any trauma recently.

Musculoskeletal: Right elbow pain.
Cardiovascular: Grade 3 systolic ejection murmur.
Respiratory: Mild intermittent asthma.
note.objective_exam:

note.objective_results:

note.assessment_and_plan:

1. Acute lateral epicondylitis of the right elbow.
- Medical Reasoning: This is likely due to overuse likely from increased tennis activity which normally would be good but maybe we are overdoing it a little bit.

Ice that right elbow for 20 minutes at least 3 times per day to reduce pain and inflammation. I will also prescribe Ultram 50 mg once per day to help with your elbow pain.
- Patient Education: We discussed this today.
- Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with these recommendations.

2. Diabetes type 2.
- Medical Reasoning: His blood sugars are a little bit out of control due to eating too many Cadbury eggs during Easter weekend.
- Medical Treatment: Increase metformin to 1000 mg twice daily for the next two weeks then check blood sugar twice daily for another two weeks then we will reevaluate his blood sugar at that time as well as order hemoglobin A1c level and CBC blood test today to check those results along with chem-12 blood test as well.
- Patient Education: We discussed this today.
- Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with these recommendations.

- Medical Reasoning: His asthma remains under good control so we will continue him on Flovent twice daily and albuterol as needed without any changes at this time but he does need a refill on his albuterol so I have written him a prescription for that refill which he can pick up at his pharmacy today if needed.
- Medical Treatment: Continue Flovent twice daily and albuterol as tolerated until further notice along with prescription refill for albuterol today if needed from pharmacy today if needed.
- Patient Education: We discussed this today.
- Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with these recommendations.

note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Sandra Williams is a 68-year-old female who presents today for evaluation of kidney stones. She reports that she had some kidney stones in the past and has been experiencing pain. She went to the emergency room last week, but now she thinks she is doing a little bit better. She denies blood in her urine and pain today. She was given Percocet for pain at the hospital.

Medical Reasoning:
- The patient did have kidney stones but they appear to have passed this time around.
- Her blood pressure was elevated at 150/90 mm Hg today, however, it was normal at home previously when measured with a home blood pressure cuff about 2-3 times per week. I recommended that we obtain a urinalysis and urine culture to rule out infection as well as obtain a referral to urology for further evaluation of recurrent kidney stones.
- Her A1c was 6.7 last time we saw her, which is slightly elevated from when she was first diagnosed with type 2 diabetes one year ago. We discussed starting her on metformin again as well as checking her blood sugars daily to help us get her off of all medications eventually.
- The patient has been having issues with insomnia but has tried meditation apps which have helped somewhat. We discussed proper sleep hygiene including turning off electronics before bed and making sure the room is dark and cool.
- The patient does not want to take any sleeping pills so I prescribed melatonin as needed for insomnia.
- Medical Treatment:
- Obtain urinalysis and urine culture today.
- Obtain referral to urology today.
- Continue taking Norvasc 2.5 mg daily as prescribed by pharmacy.
- Continue taking Metformin 500 mg daily as prescribed by pharmacy.

Asthma.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Betty Lewis is a 66-year-old female who presents to the clinic today for worsening asthma symptoms. The patient reports that she has been experiencing shortness of breath, wheezing, and coughing almost every month for the past 6 months. She notes that she has been going to urgent care and her primary care provider frequently for these symptoms. She has been prescribed steroids and antibiotics in the past. She also mentions that she has had to go to the emergency department once due to her asthma symptoms when she was younger.

The patient reports that her asthma flares up when she gets sick with a cold. She also notes that she had an exacerbation about a month ago. She mentions that she has tried hiking but is concerned about her coughing and wheezing.

The patient denies smoking cigarettes or marijuana on a regular basis, vaping or e-cigarette use, or exposure to airborne particulates such as smoking in bars.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Respiratory: Shortness of breath, wheezing, coughing.
• Constitutional: Fatigue.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm without any murmurs, rubs, gallops or ectopic beats.
Respiratory: Diminished lung sounds throughout with occasional expiratory wheeze bilaterally.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Pulmonary function test obtained today is consistent with asthma.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Betty Lewis is a 66-year-old female who presents today for worsening asthma symptoms.
• Asthma.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient’s symptoms are consistent with moderate intermittent asthma based on her history of exacerbations and daily use of albuterol inhaler. Her pulmonary function test was consistent with asthma as well.
- Medical Treatment: I have started her on Flovent one hundred ten micrograms one puff twice per day which will help prevent daily symptoms and reduce the need for rescue inhaler use. She can continue using Ventolin inhaler as needed every 4-6 hours p.r.n. We will also work on an asthma action plan together so we know what to do based on her symptoms.
- Patient Education: We discussed the importance of being consistent with her inhaled steroid inhaler as well as how to avoid triggers such as cats at her aunt’s house.

Right knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Kenneth King is a 44-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of right knee pain. The onset of his symptoms began approximately 5 days ago when he was out on his boat skiing and did a jump and twisted when he landed. He denies hearing anything pop or feeling anything pop at the time. He was able to get out of the water by himself but it was very sore to climb up and any kind of squatting or bending is really pretty sore. He has never injured this knee before. He is a frequent water skier.

The patient reports that he has been taking lisinopril 20 mg once a day for his hypertension. His blood pressure at home has been about 125/80 most of the days. He denies any side effects from lisinopril.

The patient reports that he has been taking Aleve twice a day for pain relief, as well as applying ice to his right knee.

He denies any numbness or tingling in his foot.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports right knee pain.
Neurological: Denies numbness or tingling in his foot.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neck: No lymphadenopathy appreciated.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs appreciated.
Respiratory: Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally.

There is decreased range of motion bilaterally with negative varus and valgus tests, negative Lachman sign, palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Lisinopril 20 mg once a day.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Right knee pain.
- Medical Reasoning: I agree with you that you had quite an injury to your knee and do have some fluid in your knee there and just some inflammation which I think we need to talk about today.
- Medical Treatment Plan: We will order an x-ray of your right knee just to make sure that we're not missing any broken bones which I don't think we are but what's good about this particular injury is that people typically heal quite well from this and they typically don't need surgery. We can just go ahead and refer you to physical therapy to strengthen those muscles around your knee so that you don't have another injury today. I would prescribe meloxicam fifteen milligrams once a day which will help take down the swelling and help with some of the pain. You only have to take it once a day and it won't really cause any upset stomach or anything like that today.
- Patient Education/ Counseling: We discussed my medical treatment plan today, as well as recommended additional testing today including an x-ray of your right knee today.
- Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with my recommended medical treatment plan today.

Neurological: No focal deficits noted.

note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Incidentally found right upper lobe lung nodule.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient presents today for evaluation of an incidentally found right upper lobe lung nodule. Given his smoking history, I have recommended that we proceed with a PET-CT to determine if this nodule is metabolically active. If it does appear to be metabolically active, we will proceed with video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery to remove the nodule along with a small portion of his lung tissue for biopsy.
- Patient Education and Counseling: I have counseled the patient regarding his diagnosis and recommended treatment plan today. We discussed the risks and benefits associated with each option as well as alternative treatment options available to him at this time. He understands and agrees with the recommended course of action today.
- Medical Treatment Plan:
PFTs (Pulmonary Function Tests) - Baseline for your lung function.
PET-CT - To determine if this nodule is metabolically active meaning if it lights up it can suggest that it's cancer or inflammatory.
Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery - To remove this along with a very small portion of your lung tissue for biopsy.

He notes that it feels like he needs to wash down solid foods on occasion, but liquids seem to go down fine. The patient denies coughing with this issue.

The patient denies blood in his stools or vomiting at all.

His weight has not changed.

He denies chest pain or shortness of breath with this issue.

Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain or shortness of breath.

The patient presents today for evaluation of dysphagia. His symptoms have been present for approximately 4-5 weeks and are worse with solids than liquids. His weight has not changed from prior visits but he does report feeling good overall otherwise since we last saw him ago when we discussed improving diet and exercise recommendations for his diabetes management as well as reviewing his current medications including metformin 500 mg twice daily which was last checked at that time at an A1C level of 7.4% which was within target range based on our discussion at that time however we did discuss the importance of monitoring blood glucose levels more frequently than once per day to ensure glycemic control remains stable as well as discussing Norvasc for hypertension management which appears to be working well based on today's blood pressure readings in office today were within target range however there were some fluctuations noted between home monitoring versus office monitoring so I recommended continuing Norvasc until further notice while also recommending additional lifestyle modifications such as increased physical activity and dietary changes to help improve overall cardiovascular health including weight loss if applicable given the patient's BMI was slightly elevated at prior visits but currently stable based on recent measurements taken during this visit today I recommended ordering another A1C test to assess glycemic control again after reviewing recent dietary habits with the patient he reported sticking to his Lateral malleolar fracture of the right ankle.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Evaluation of facial pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Anthony Miller is a 54-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of facial pain. The onset of his symptoms began approximately 2-3 months ago and has been gradually worsening. He describes the pain as stabbing and shooting in the right cheekbone area. He denies any sensory loss, numbness, or tingling in the right cheek. He does report left-sided facial pain, however, he denies any left-sided facial weakness. The patient reports headaches but denies any history of migraines. He has tried ibuprofen and motrin but these have not helped with his symptoms. The patient has also tried applying Tiger Balm to the area but this did not help either.

The patient denies any history of multiple sclerosis or brain tumors. He does report occasional headaches that he treats with Tylenol.

Pain is described as a 10/10 when it comes on and usually resolves within a few minutes but can last up to an hour.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Neurological: Denies vision changes or weakness in right eye.
• Head: Reports headaches.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neurological: Examination of cranial nerves is intact bilaterally. No facial weakness noted on examination.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

MRI of the head was reviewed today by Dr. Cruz and appears to have small blood vessel that is abutting and perhaps even pinching the trigeminal nerve. The trigeminal nerve is a nerve that comes from the brainstem that goes out to the face and provides sensation from the face. This may be causing trigeminal neuralgia.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Anthony Miller is a 54-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of facial pain.

Medical Reasoning:
MRI of the head was reviewed today by Dr. Cruz and appears to have small blood vessel that is abutting and perhaps even pinching the trigeminal nerve which may be causing trigeminal neuralgia.
Medical Treatment:
I have discussed this with him today and we have decided to start him on tegretol (carbamazepine) initially for 1 month to see if this helps with his symptoms. If after 1 month his pain continues we can discuss surgical options further at that time.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Right knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Michelle King is a 44-year-old female who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of right knee pain. The onset of her symptoms began 1 week ago when she was skiing in Vermont and caught her ski when she was coming off the lift and fell. She was unable to bear weight on her right knee at that time. She denies any numbness or tingling in her toes, but does report that she has some pain with straightening her right knee. She denies any leg edema in the ankle. She reports that she is able to bend her right knee immediately after the injury but not really now.

She reports that she is otherwise healthy and denies a history of high blood pressure or diabetes.

SOCIAL HISTORY

The patient reports that she is very active with skiing and taking care of her 4-year-old twins. Her husband works a job where he is gone quite a bit.

MEDICATIONS

The patient reports that she takes ibuprofen for pain.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports right knee pain.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm without murmurs.
Respiratory: Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Musculoskeletal: Examination of the right knee reveals edema and effusion over the right knee. There is pain to palpation over the lateral aspect of the right knee, decreased flexion and extension, positive Lachman's test, palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, no leg edema in the ankle.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Right knee pain.

She reports that she is able to bend her right knee immediately after the injury but not really now.
Medical Treatment Plan: I have reviewed this case with Michelle King today and we discussed conservative treatment options including ibuprofen for pain management as well as bracing to support her right knee while it heals. We also discussed obtaining an MRI of the right knee to further evaluate for possible ACL rupture or other soft tissue damage from this injury. We discussed surgical options if conservative treatment fails at a later date.
Patient Education: I have also educated Michelle King on proper home exercises for strengthening and stretching as well as recommended physical therapy if needed.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Neck pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Brandon Green is a pleasant 46-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of neck pain. The patient was involved in 4 motor vehicle accidents. He was fine after the first two accidents. The third motor vehicle accident is when his neck and back pain began. He was in therapy following the second accident. He had surgery after his third accident. He was seen at a pain clinic secondary to neck and back pain.

The patient reports that he has been experiencing neck pain since February of this year, which is when he was coming home from the pain clinic because his neck hurt and his back hurt. The patient denies any numbness or dizziness, but does report experiencing headaches and occasional visual disturbances.

Pain is described as sharp, incapacitating, and constant. The patient rates his arm being cut off by a chainsaw severe on a scale of 1 to 10.

The patient has been prescribed fentanyl recently but has not gotten a prescription for several weeks.

The patient denies any stiffness, but reports that it hurts when he moves his neck from side to side. He also reports that it hurts to bend forward and backwards.

The patient reports that he has bruising and swelling sometimes.

He also reports fatigue since the accident.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neck: Pain on palpation both on the bony process and on the muscle.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-rays of the neck were obtained today and reviewed in office today.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Brandon Green is a pleasant 46-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of neck pain.

I have reviewed the x-rays of the neck obtained today, which do not reveal any fractures. I have discussed this with him today as well as reviewed all of his symptoms with him today.
I have recommended we try treating this conservatively at this time as we are not seeing any signs of fracture on imaging today. We will start with Robaxin 1500 mg every 6-8 hours initially to help relax the muscles in the area and take off some tension from his neck to help with his pain.
We will also refer him to physical therapy for additional treatment options once we review his MRI results today.
If Robaxin does not help with his symptoms, we can refer him to pain medicine for additional options including local injections into the area or possibly even fentanyl if needed at that point in time.

Follow-up of chronic problems.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Carolyn Garcia is a 49-year-old female who presents today for follow-up of her chronic problems. She reports that her osteoarthritis has been flaring up a little bit lately, primarily in her right elbow. She has been sitting at the computer, at the desk more in the office and does not know if it is being stagnant in that position all day which has increased flare-ups for that. She also reports that she has been typing all day versus writing, so it flares up in both elbows. She denies any other joint pain. She does report numbness and tingling in her hands when she is typing for long periods of time, but tries to shake out her arms to relieve that sensation.

She also reports that she has had a history of gout. The last episode she had was about 3 months ago and she had some inflammation of her toe. She states that the medication prescribed by me really controlled it and she has not seen a flare-up since.

She also reports that she has had psoriasis which is under control too.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports right elbow pain with right olecranon bursa tenderness and effusion with pain with pronation and supination as well as pain with flexion and extension of the right arm.
Neurological: Reports numbness and tingling in her hands when typing for long periods of time.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Left elbow pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Anna Morris is a 26-year-old female who presents today for evaluation of left elbow pain. She reports that she has been sitting at her desk a lot for work and typing all day, and after work it is difficult for her to open and close her left elbow. She describes the pain as stiffness and pain. She also notes that there is swelling at the tip of her left elbow. She denies any numbness or tingling in her hands, but does report a little bit of weakness in her arm. She denies any fever or chills.

The patient reports that she last had a seizure a year ago, but she is currently taking Keppra 500 mg twice daily to control her epilepsy. She has been seeing a therapist for depression since last year, but she still feels down and stressed. The patient reports that she had endoscopy last year which showed gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, and she has been taking Protonix 40 mg once daily before meals to treat this.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Denies fever or chills.
• Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain or shortness of breath.
• Respiratory: Denies dyspnea on exertion.
• Gastrointestinal: Reports nasal congestion from allergies.
• Musculoskeletal: Reports left elbow pain.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neurological:
- Examination of the head, neck, and upper extremities reveals no focal neurological deficits.
- Sensation to light touch is intact distally in both upper extremities.
- Motor strength in all four extremities with the exception of right radial pulse which is palpable bilaterally.
- Reflexes are 2+ in the right upper extremity with normal tone bilaterally in the lower extremities.
- No evidence of spasticity or ataxia noted.
- No evidence of cerebellar dysfunction noted.
- No evidence of cranial nerve deficits noted except for right facial weakness which was present prior to this visit.

Musculoskeletal:
- Examination of the left arm reveals erythema and edema at the tip of the left elbow. There is tenderness to palpation over the olecranon process bilaterally. The area is warm to palpation. There is no active or passive range of motion with pain with flexion and extension.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Left arm x-ray obtained today revealed no evidence of an elbow fracture.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Anna Morris is a 26-year-old female who presents today for evaluation of left elbow pain. She was diagnosed with olecranon bursitis based on examination findings today as well as radiographic findings from today's x-ray which revealed no evidence of an elbow fracture. We discussed conservative treatment options including icing the area, resting, and using a pillow for support while sleeping as well as meloxicam 15 mg once daily for pain management. We discussed medical treatment options including oral steroids if needed after trying conservative measures without success. We also discussed referral to physical therapy if needed after trying conservative measures without success.

She continues to take Keppra 500 mg twice daily for epilepsy management as prescribed by neurology today due to continued seizure control despite starting therapy last year. We discussed medical treatment options including adding Lexapro 10 mg once daily due to continued depressive symptoms despite therapy since last year; however, we will continue with therapy until we see how she responds to Lexapro before considering medical treatment options further at this time.

She continues to take Protonix 40 mg once daily before meals due to gastritis and peptic ulcer disease as prescribed by gastroenterology today due to continued improvement since endoscopy last year which showed gastritis and peptic ulcer disease resolving after protonix treatment was initiated.

She has been feeling tired, really lacking energy, and has swollen joints in her elbows, which hurts. She has had body aches. She is still taking metformin daily.

The patient's elevated Lyme titer suggests active infection with Lyme disease; however, we will need further testing before initiating treatment for this diagnosis as there are other possibilities for this elevation including other tick-borne diseases such as ehrlichiosis or babesiosis as well as other causes such as autoimmune disease or medication side effects.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus is well controlled at this time with metformin daily; however, we will order an HbA1c today to ensure that she continues to be doing well on this medication.
The patient's blood pressure appears stable at this time; however, we will order a lipid panel today to assess for any dyslipidemia which may be contributing to her hypertension.
We discussed treatment options for Lyme disease today including doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 3 weeks; however, I will follow up with an infectious disease specialist before starting any antibiotics due to concerns regarding tick-borne diseases other than Lyme disease such as ehrlichiosis or babesiosis as well as medication side effects from doxycycline such as photosensitivity or gastrointestinal upset.
The patient understands all treatment options.

Evaluation of high blood sugar.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Hannah Phillips is a 52-year-old female who presents today for evaluation of a high blood sugar. She reports that she has been eating a lot of sweets recently due to the holidays. She felt fine at first, but has started to feel light-headed and sees spots after a couple of weeks. She went to the emergency room and was treated with IV fluids and told to cut out extra sweets and get back into her normal routine. She is still staying with her family, where her mom and grandmother are big bakers, so she is concerned about getting into a routine there.

She denies fever, chills, chest pain or shortness of breath, abdominal pain, burning when urinating, joint pain or muscle aches.

She does have osteoarthritis.

She has had atrial fibrillation for many years. She reports that she feels her heart racing only when she is really anxious. She has been doing well with her reflux symptoms since starting protonix 40 mg once daily.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Denies fever or chills.
• Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain or shortness of breath.
• Respiratory: Denies dyspnea on exertion.
• Gastrointestinal: Denies abdominal pain or burning when urinating.
• Musculoskeletal: Denies joint pain or muscle aches.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Cardiovascular: Irregular rate and rhythm. No carotid bruits heard.
Respiratory: Lungs are clear bilaterally.
Gastrointestinal: Soft abdomen without edema in lower extremities.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Glucose elevated; HbA1c elevated.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

High blood sugar.
Diabetes mellitus type 2 is suspected based on elevated glucose levels and hemoglobin A1c levels. We are not sure if this is type 1 diabetes mellitus at this time as patients can develop type 1 diabetes mellitus in their mid-twenties as well. We will order complete metabolic panel labs today to work up this possibility. I have started her on metformin 500 mg twice daily today to help keep her blood sugars down while we await the results from the labs today. If some of the autoimmune labs come back showing that she has an autoimmune disorder meaning that she would have type 1 diabetes mellitus then we would have to go ahead and put her on insulin at that time but I am holding off until we have those results back today. We will also order a refill on metoprolol 25 mg twice daily today as well as continue protonix 40 mg once daily for reflux symptoms today.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Yearly asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergy follow-up.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Emily Hernandez is a 20-year-old female who presents today for a yearly follow-up for asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergies. She was switched from Symbicort to Wixela due to insurance changes since her last office visit in April 2020. She also uses Zyrtec in the spring, summer, and fall for her seasonal allergy symptoms, which tend to work well. She also has known peanut allergy; she does tolerate almonds and cashews. Her asthma Control Test (ACT) score is 21.

The patient reports that she has been doing well since her last office visit. She notes that she has been trying to reduce smoking and vaping in preparation for joining the military. She has been trying to reduce smoking and vaping in preparation for joining the military. She has been trying to reduce smoking and vaping in preparation for joining the military.

She reports that she has not had any urgent care or ER visits for breathing over the past year.

She is currently enlisted with the army and hopes to be enlisted early spring of 2022. She will need to complete some exertional tests at that time.

She reports that she had an allergic reaction to peanuts when cleaning out a car at Enterprise Rent-a-Car last year. Since then, she has become more cautious about peanuts and nuts in general.

She notes that she has been vaping and smoking cigarettes but is trying to cut down on both of these habits.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath or wheezing.
• Skin: Reports hives after exposure to peanuts.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
• Ears: Normal appearance bilaterally with minimal cerumen noted bilaterally.
• Nose: No nasal polyps or congestion.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS
• Spirometry: The patient's spirometry results are consistent with her prior results from 2 years ago but appear slightly better today.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Emily Hernandez is a 20-year-old female who presents today for a yearly follow-up for asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergies.

Medical Reasoning:
The patient's spirometry results are consistent with her prior results from 2 years ago but appear slightly better today. This may be due to reduced exposure to smoke this year compared to previous years when there were many fires throughout the area. Her ACT score is 21 which indicates good control of her asthma symptoms at this time.
Medical Treatment:
The patient will continue using Wixela Inhub 250 mcg-50 mcg/dose powder for inhalation as needed once daily in the morning and once at night as tolerated. We discussed options today regarding treatment options moving forward including switching back to alvesco inhaler twice daily as an alternative option if Wixela does not work well enough for her at this time. We discussed that we would need repeat spirometry testing in 4 months after starting alvesco inhaler twice daily if we decide on this option moving forward so we can document improvement in lung function at that time. The patient will continue using Zyrtec as needed during peak allergy season as tolerated. We discussed that it would be beneficial if she could try reducing her use of Zyrtec during non-allergy seasons as well so we can minimize side effects from long-term use of this medication.
Patient Education:
The patient was counseled regarding continued avoidance of peanuts due to severe anaphylactic reaction history with ingestion of peanuts; however, she does tolerate almonds and cashews due to cross-reactivity between these nuts and peanuts.
Patient Agreements:
The patient understands all medical recommendations provided today.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Resistant hypertension.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Jordan Roberts is a 49-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of resistant hypertension. He reports that he has had issues with his blood pressure since he was young. He has been on a new medication about a month ago, which is Benicar HCT 40 mg/25 mg. He is currently taking Amlodipine 10 mg daily. He has been checking his blood pressure at home every day, and it has been running at about 146 to 155 lately. He denies any palpitations since the emergency room visit in March.

The patient reports that he drinks coffee and does not eat breakfast on occasion, which he believes may have contributed to his high blood pressure in the emergency room.

The patient reports that he does try to walk on the treadmill when he can.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: Hypertension.
Family History: Several family members positive for hypertension.

MEDICATIONS

Benicar HCT 40 mg/25 mg; Amlodipine 10 mg daily.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmurs, gallops, or rubs heard.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Thyroid profile from 03/01/2021 was normal.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Resistant hypertension.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient is currently on three medications at maximum dose and his blood pressure is still not down. The question is what do we need to do to get his blood pressure down.
- Medical Treatment: We discussed adding spironolactone to his regimen today. We will need to monitor his potassium and sodium levels as this can cause electrolyte disturbances with spironolactone. We will also need to monitor his electrolytes in two weeks after starting the new medication. If the new med does not work, we will refer him to the resistant hypertension clinic for further evaluation of secondary causes of hypertension.
- Patient Education: I have discussed with him the potential side effects of spironolactone including gynecomastia and electrolyte disturbances. I have also discussed with him that carvedilol would be an alternative but it has potential for erectile dysfunction.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Return visit for IBS with functional abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Brittany Edwards is a pleasant 32-year-old female who was last seen in August of 2019 with flares of abdominal pain, who was diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) that was treated with Bentyl. She had a previous prescription for Reglan that she received from the emergency room that she used as needed for nausea. She was instructed to start a low dose fiber supplement, such as Citrucel, daily, probiotics to help with gas and bloating, Bentyl up to four times daily for intestinal cramping, and stop Reglan and use Zofran as needed. Neuromodulators such as Elavil and Buspar were discussed but not started.

She reports that she has been going out to eat some on Friday nights and Saturday nights and that she has had some spicy foods or shrimp. She states that her gut probably does not always appreciate that. She has been getting both lower belly cramps and upper belly nausea. She notes that she is starting to notice it is between 2-3 times a day now. Her stools are formed. When she eats pasta at Friday's restaurant, she usually does not have any issues. However, when she drinks alcohol or eats fried chicken today, she experiences more diarrhea.

She notes that her symptoms are worse when drinking alcohol or eating fried chicken today.

She reports that her symptoms are better when drinking water instead of sodas.

The patient denies any constipation.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: History of high stress.
Psychiatric: History of poor eating habits; history of poor sleeping habits.
Family: History of high stress.

CURRENT MEDICATIONS

Bentyl; Zofran; Elavil 25 mg at bedtime; Citrucel; Probiotics.

note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Brittany Edwards is a pleasant female with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and functional abdominal pain aggravated by high stress, poor eating habits, and poor sleeping habits. I have encouraged dietary and lifestyle modifications as well as starting a neuromodulator such as Elavil 25 mg at bedtime for IBS. She can use Bentyl 20 mg as needed 30-45 minutes prior to eating out at a restaurant. She can also use Zofran if needed. However, I have encouraged her to reduce greasy and fatty foods and alcohol consumption. We discussed the possibility of long-term medication options including Elavil which would take the place of Bentyl or Zofran if symptoms are not improving with dietary modifications alone. We discussed the side effects associated with Elavil including sedation which may impact her ability to drive safely in the morning after taking it at night before bed. We discussed this option further today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today in detail today.
We reviewed her current medications including Bentyl which will be refilled through mychart email tomorrow morning after we finish our visit together this afternoon.
She can use Citrucel twice daily for regularity if needed during the week or before going out on weekends if diarrhea is anticipated due to alcohol consumption or spicy foods eaten at Friday's restaurant. If she experiences abdominal pain while drinking alcohol or eating fried chicken again tomorrow, we will discuss additional treatment options including Elavil tonight after our visit together this afternoon.
I have recommended probiotics for gas/bloating management as well as Zofran if needed due to nausea from alcohol consumption only prior to consuming alcohol rather than ahead of time since it may cause drowsiness upon waking up the next morning after taking it at night before bed while driving safely during the day is important for me personally.
