note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Follow-up for hypertension.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Amanda Taylor is a 72-year-old female who presents for follow-up of hypertension. She reports that she has been drinking alcohol 4 to 5 days per week to excess. She denies tobacco use, substance abuse, and skin is moist. She is alert, pleasant, in no acute distress.

She reports that she last had a drink on Monday. She has been abstinent for 2 days. She has been drinking for a while and reports that she drinks hard alcohol 4 to 5 times per week.

She reports that she is taking her lisinopril 20 mg once daily and hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg once daily as prescribed. She states that she only takes half of the lisinopril dose due to lethargy and headaches in the past, but feels much better since taking the full dose.

She denies chest tightness or pressure or shortness of breath with her current medications.

She reports that her blood pressure checks at home in the morning are lower than in the evening, where she runs anywhere from 130 to 145/95 to 100 on the bottom. In the evenings if she sits there for a while and then takes it, it goes down. In the mornings it is generally more normal where it is supposed to be.

She also states that she takes her medicine in the morning when she gets up instead of in the evening.

The patient denies fever, cough, shortness of breath or sore throat.

The patient has received her coronavirus vaccine on February 9th.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Cardiovascular: Unlabored breathing. Cardiac rhythm regular. No murmurs, gallops or JVP elevation.
Respiratory: Chest clear to percussion and auscultation.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Alcohol use disorder.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient drinks alcohol four to five days per week to excess which may be contributing to her hypertension as well as causing other adverse effects such as lethargy and headaches. Her blood pressure checks at home are higher than expected which may be due to alcohol consumption as well as stress from trying to stop drinking.
- Patient Education: We discussed naltrexone which was previously discussed during our last visit. The patient understands this medication will block some of the brain receptors that alcohol stimulates and tricks the brain into thinking it does not need alcohol thereby cutting down urges. The patient understands this medication can be taken as an injectable form once a month or as a daily pill but prefers an injectable form due to ease of administration and lack of risk of forgetting doses.
- Medical Treatment: We discussed side effects including nausea, headache, dizziness, anxiety, tiredness and trouble sleeping but these are generally mild and should resolve within a few days after administration of naltrexone injection. We reviewed potential benefits including cessation of alcohol use which would likely result in improvement in blood pressure control with subsequent reduction in cardiovascular risk factors such as hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia.
- Patient Agreements: The patient understands all recommendations today and agrees with treatment plan.

Thomas Nelson is a 72-year-old male who presents today for ongoing management of rheumatoid arthritis. He reports that his right knee was injected with a steroid injection on 03/04/2021. Since then, he has been experiencing swelling in his right knee and leg. He rates his pain as a 3 out of 10, but typically it is around 6. The swelling has been present for about two months. He notes that the swelling was just in the knee before, but now it is also present in the leg. He has been wearing compression socks regularly, but they have not helped with the swelling. The patient reports that he has slowed down a little bit and finds some things too fast due to the pain. When it really hurts, he has to sit for a while and then get up, which is difficult due to stiffness in his leg. He states that after a little while, it loosens up, but getting up is difficult at first. The patient reports that he has been taking his medication regularly and notes that he started Celebrex 2 months ago. However, since starting Celebrex, his swelling has returned.

The patient denies any difficulty with ambulation or activities of daily living due to pain.

The patient denies any difficulty with sleep.

The patient denies any fevers or chills.

The patient denies any weight loss or unintentional weight gain.

Patient reports no urinary symptoms.

Patient reports no bowel symptoms.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Perioral dermatitis.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Jacqueline Miller is a 40-year-old female who presents today for the evaluation of perioral dermatitis. She has been using doxycycline cream twice daily for the past two weeks, but she has noticed that her rash has plateaued and is not continuing to improve. She discontinued breastfeeding and started taking doxycycline at that time. She was prescribed MetroCream and sulfacetamide wash, but she stopped using MetroCream because she read about it online and got worried. She has been using the sulfacetamide wash twice daily, but she does not feel that it is drying her out too much. The patient denies using any other lotions or cleansers.

The patient reports that she started taking doxycycline once a day last week, which seemed to improve her rash, but it has plateaued again. She notes that when she used the sulfacetamide wash twice daily, she felt sun sensitive and had to take precautions with sun exposure.

The patient denies any other symptoms.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Skin: erythema, papules.
• Eyes: dryness.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Ears, Nose, Mouth: Fitzpatrick skin type IV. There are a few faint erythematous papules on bilateral medial cheeks.
note.objective_results: RESULTS
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Jacqueline Miller is a 40-year-old female who presents today for the evaluation of perioral dermatitis.

Medical Reasoning:
- Perioral dermatitis is typically treated with topical antibiotics such as doxycycline or clindamycin. However, due to her breastfeeding status, we discussed alternative options such as elidel cream or tacrolimus ointment.
- The patient’s rash has plateaued after starting doxycycline once daily last week. We discussed this with the patient and decided to continue doxycycline twice daily until resolution of her rash.
- The patient discontinued breastfeeding and started taking doxycycline at that time. We discussed this with the patient and advised her that it is safe to continue breastfeeding while taking elidel cream or tacrolimus ointment.
- The patient was prescribed MetroCream and sulfacetamide washes for treatment of perioral dermatitis. However, she discontinued MetroCream because she read about it online and got worried. We discussed this with the patient and advised her that there are no risks associated with topical use of these medications.
- The patient’s current treatment plan includes continuing use of the same face wash as before as well as metro cream after face washing. We recommended increasing use of doxycycline to twice daily until resolution of her rash.
- We recommended tacrolimus ointment for treatment of perioral dermatitis due to its low risk profile compared to oral antibiotics such as doxycycline or clindamycin.
- We recommended vanicream for moisturizing purposes due to its low risk profile compared to anti-aging products or plant-based products.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Abdominal pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Michael Rodriguez is a pleasant 47-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of abdominal pain. The onset of his pain began several weeks ago and has been worsening. He denies any fevers, but reports nausea and vomiting. He rates his pain as an 8 on a scale of 0 to 10, with 10 being the worst pain he has ever experienced. The pain is located in the right upper quadrant of his abdomen and radiates to his right shoulder blade. The patient states that the pain is severe and comes and goes, but when it does come it is severe. The patient reports that the pain typically occurs immediately after eating, but can also occur a couple of hours after eating.

The patient reports that he has been managing his type 2 diabetes with diet and exercise. He notes that he was previously worse with his diet before being diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, but since then he has cut back on sugar and started a keto diet which has resulted in weight loss of approximately 25 pounds over the last three months. He notes that since starting this diet, his symptoms have improved as well as his blood sugars.

The patient denies any family history of gallbladder disease.

SOCIAL HISTORY

The patient enjoys nature photography.

FAMILY HISTORY

Both parents have had cholecystectomies.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm without murmurs, rubs or clicks.
Respiratory: Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Gastrointestinal: Soft non-distended abdomen; positive for some slight guarding to the right upper quadrant; no rebound tenderness.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Abdominal ultrasound obtained at an outside facility shows multiple gallstones present in the gallbladder with some mild thickening. The common bile duct size is within normal limits at 4.1 mm.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Medical Reasoning: Michael Rodriguez is a pleasant 47-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of abdominal pain. The onset of his pain began several weeks ago and has been worsening. He denies any fevers, but reports nausea and vomiting. His blood pressure was 128/88 mmHg today, respiratory rate was 16 breaths per minute, heart rate was 68 beats per minute, oxygen saturation was 99% on room air, and body temperature was afebrile today which is a good thing.
Medical Treatment: I do believe you have some mild cholecystitis with gallstones I do not appreciate any frank obstruction but it looks like your gallbladder is inflamed and it looks like that's happened maybe over the last few weeks since you've been having those symptoms now since you have not had any improvement with dietary modifications I am going to make the recommendation that we do remove your gallbladder and I would like to perform a laparoscopic cholecystectomy now what that means is I'll make a few small incisions and insert a scope with some of those instruments that's going to remove that gallbladder through one of those little bitty incisions now the surgery is going to take about an hour to an hour-and-a-half and you'll probably spend the night in the hospital because we just want to monitor you post procedure to make sure everything is okay you're still going to want to avoid those high fat foods after surgery eat foods that are going to be high in fiber now do you have any questions about what our assessment and plan is for this?
Patient Education: We discussed my recommended treatment plan today including laparoscopic cholecystectomy for mild cholecystitis with gallstones.
Patient Agreements: The patient understands my recommended medical treatment plan.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Right shoulder pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Matthew Allen is a 67-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of right shoulder pain. The onset of his symptoms began approximately 4 days ago when he was tackled while playing tackle football. He denies any numbness or tingling in his fingers, but reports that his strength is slightly diminished in his right arm. He notes that he has been avoiding lifting anything heavy, as it has been difficult for him to do so. He denies any neck pain or other joint pain in the rest of his body. The patient reports that he had an appendectomy 3 to 4 years ago.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports right shoulder pain.
Neurological: Denies numbness or tingling in the right arm.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Cervical Spine: No tenderness to palpation of the cervical spine. Full range of motion on head exam. No ecchymosis or bruising.
Musculoskeletal: Pain to palpation of the posterior shoulder at the acromioclavicular joint. Decreased abduction and adduction to about 90 degrees only. Pain with supination and pronation of the right arm. Palpable radial artery pulse.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-ray of the right shoulder reveals an acute acromioclavicular joint fracture.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Right shoulder injury for acute acromioclavicular joint fracture.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient presents today with a history of a recent fall while playing tackle football, which resulted in right shoulder pain. His examination today revealed tenderness over the acromioclavicular joint, decreased abduction and adduction to about 90 degrees only, and pain with supination and pronation of the right arm.
- Medical Treatment: I have discussed this finding with him today and we have discussed treatment options including non-operative management with a sling and oral analgesics such as meloxicam fifteen milligrams once a day, as well as referral for physical therapy to strengthen his shoulder in hopes of avoiding surgery in the future. We also discussed surgical options if needed.
- Patient Education: I have also provided education regarding conservative treatment options including bracing and oral analgesics such as meloxicam fifteen milligrams once a day, as well as referral for physical therapy to strengthen his shoulder in hopes of avoiding surgery in the future.
- Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with recommended medical treatment.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Lower back pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Jeremy Adams is a 57-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of lower back pain. The onset of his symptoms began about 4 months ago when he was moving some boxes when his son was moving out of his college dorm. He states that he really hurt his lower back at that time. He reports that he has been experiencing pain when sitting for a very short period of time, as if he is going to topple over. He also reports that he has tingling in the right toes, which resolved after about an hour. He denies any numbness or tingling in his feet at this point. The patient denies any difficulty or weakness in his legs. He does report that he experiences sharp pain in his lower back if he turns a certain way or if he rolls over in bed, but this resolves once he positions himself correctly.

The patient reports taking Tylenol and ibuprofen for pain, but notes that the ibuprofen seems to be better than Tylenol for a shorter period of time.

The patient denies fevers or chills, bowel issues, bladder issues, and incontinence.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: Right total knee arthroplasty 2 years ago, in spring of 2020.

SOCIAL HISTORY

The patient reports that he is currently working full-time.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Constitutional: Denies fevers or chills.
Musculoskeletal: Reports lower back pain.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: No bony protuberance noted on examination. No tenderness to palpation.
Lumbar Spine: Decreased flexion and extension of the lower back. Positive straight leg raise test bilaterally. Spasm of paraspinal muscles noted bilaterally.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS
X-rays of the lumbar spine were obtained today and reviewed by me today. There were no acute bony abnormalities noted.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Jeremy Adams is a 57-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of lower back pain.
Acute disk herniation.
Plan: I do believe it sounds like you have an acute disk herniation now based on your history and examination findings today. This did happen a few months ago but it sounds like that's what you had based on the fact that you're still having symptoms today. We will order a lumbar spine MRI to get a better look at what's going on with your spine today as well as continue with physical therapy through our health system to help with your symptoms today as well as prescribe meloxicam fifteen milligrams once daily to help with your pain.

After the ankle soreness went away, he began to experience right knee pain and clicking with ambulation. The patient denies any swelling or bruising at this time. He denies any numbness or tingling in his foot at this time.

The patient reports that he has fractured his 2nd toe 3 times over the last 10 years.

The patient works in sales and rides a bike for exercise.

X-rays of the right knee were reviewed today by me and I have reviewed them with you today as well. There are no acute fractures or bony abnormalities noted.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
Gregory Price is a 68-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for right knee pain.
I have reviewed x-rays of his right knee today and there are no acute fractures or bony abnormalities noted which is not surprising based on his injury pattern.
I think you do have a lateral collateral ligament strain based on your exam findings and this type of injury essentially can be healed by itself, we are not going to need to refer you to surgery or anything like that.
I want you to go ahead and start taking meloxicam fifteen milligrams once a day, I do want you to go ahead and refer you to physical therapy because if we strengthen up those muscles and areas around that injury then that will make your knee stronger it will help prevent future injuries.
You can ice it at least four times a day during the day if you would like, but honestly I have a pretty decent threshold for pain so it's not changing it by much at all, but icing does help in the morning when you first go to your desk and before bed before you go to sleep at night when you take ibuprofen so it does help with swelling overnight.
The only time I feel like they get worse is when I exert myself doing up and down like gardening in the yard or moving pots, but nothing to the point where it stayed worse than normal. We will follow up with physical therapy if your symptoms continue worsening we might have to consider an MRI.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Non-healing right foot ulcer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Christina Cooper is a 77-year-old female who presents today for evaluation of a non-healing right foot ulcer. The patient reports that the ulcer has been present for approximately 1 year. She notes that she initially had a little blister on her right foot, which she picked at and it became infected. She then went to her primary care provider (PCP) who prescribed Keflex antibiotics, which seemed to help. However, the ulcer has not healed and she has been taking antibiotics for the past 5 months. She denies any trauma to the foot.

The patient reports that she is doing well except for her non-healing right foot ulcer. She notes that she has lost sensation in her right foot due to diabetes and that she is experiencing increased drainage from the wound as well as fatigue.

The patient denies fever or chills.

She reports that she will be walking around at the zoo this weekend and eating out, but does not follow up with her PCP regarding these activities.

She reports that her blood sugars have been running better than they were previously but are still in the 200s. Her last hemoglobin A1C was 10%.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Fatigue.
• Musculoskeletal: Pain in right foot.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

CV: No murmurs, gallops, or rubs heard.
Respiratory: No wheezes, rales, or rhonchi appreciated.
Cardiovascular: No edema in lower extremities noted.
Gastrointestinal: No abdominal pain or distention noted.
Musculoskeletal: Examination of the right foot reveals a 1 by 2 centimeter two inch circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot proximal to the fifth metatarsophalangeal joint. There is minimal granulation tissue present with yellow slough. There is no surrounding erythema or cellulitis and there is no evidence of fluid collection. There is no evidence of necrosis around the wound site and there is no odor present. There is no bony exposure.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-ray of the right foot was performed today and revealed no evidence of osteomyelitis.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Christina Cooper is a 77-year-old female who presents today for evaluation of a non-healing right foot ulcer.
• Medical Reasoning:
- The patient presents with a diabetic foot ulcer which likely explains her neuropathy as well as why it has not healed despite antibiotic treatment. The patient also presents with increased drainage from her wound as well as fatigue which may be related to diabetes control but could also be related to infection or poor nutrition due to lack of appetite from eating out this weekend at the zoo.
- The x-ray was negative for osteomyelitis so we can continue with conservative management including debridement and colagenase ointment application until we see improvement in wound healing.
- We will order an ABI to determine if there is adequate blood flow to heal this wound.
• Medical Treatment:
The patient will follow up with me in 2 weeks after debridement and ointment application have been completed.

note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Jose Thompson is a 75-year-old male who presents today for a follow-up visit. His current medical treatment plan includes aspirin, Brilinta, Crestor, Metoprolol 50 mg once a day, and fish oil. The patient has been taking the aspirin and fish oil but has stopped taking the Crestor due to muscle aches. We discussed this today and I advised him to continue on aspirin for the rest of his life as well as Brilinta for another six months to help prevent stent clogging. We discussed that every so often the stents can become narrowed again but we will continue to monitor him closely with further testing if needed. We also discussed that we will need to continue monitoring his kidney function as well as diet due to his diabetes.

Regarding medication side effects, we discussed that he may be experiencing dizziness with standing up quickly which could be related to either his heart attack or medication side effects. I advised him that this could be related to beta-blocker side effects and recommended Tylenol for headaches instead of Motrin or Advil which he had stopped taking due to kidney function issues.

Regarding stage three chronic kidney disease, I recommended referral for diabetic education as well as an appointment with Dr. Miller for further evaluation of kidney function.

Regarding diabetes management, I recommended another hemoglobin A1c test and referral for dietary education from our dietitian.
We also discussed psychiatric referral given his recent history of heart attack and current mood state.

Elevated cholesterol.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Julie Cruz is a 17-year-old non-binary immensipated minor with no significant past medical history presents for evaluation of newly diagnosed hypercholesterolemia. She reports that she went for her annual checkup and they checked her cholesterol level, which was elevated. She was told to come in today to see me.

The patient reports that she enjoys being outside and riding her bike on trails. She has been keeping pretty active during the week. She tries to eat pretty clean diet most days, but she really does like chocolate chip cookies. She had a bike ride over the weekend with some friends.

She denies any issues with growing up or with her bones feeling okay. She has decided about two years ago that she is more of a non-gender and has been living as such.

The patient denies any history of heart disease or sudden death in her family's early years. Her grandparents told her that she had a cousin who died at age 44 or 45 and they think he had a heart attack.

She does not smoke at home, but one of her friends smokes occasionally.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Cardiovascular: Endorse chest pain.
Musculoskeletal: Endorse joint pain.

Neurological: No signs of thyromegaly.
note.objective_results:

Cholesterol level was elevated at 210.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Elevated cholesterol.
• Medical Reasoning: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that all children be screened once they become between ages 9 and 11 and again between ages 17 and 20. Studies have shown a link between high cholesterol and premature heart attacks.
• Medical Treatment Plan: We reviewed the results of your cholesterol level today, which was elevated at 210. We will order a full cholesterol panel today to rule out other causes for the high cholesterol levels. We will also check glucose, complete metabolic panel, thyroid studies, liver panels, and perform genetic testing to see if this problem is familial or secondary cause. We will also follow up with a well-balanced diet including variety of foods lower in saturated fat and sugars. I want you to follow this diet plan and meet with a nutritionist who can give you information about what kind of foods to eat today. Continue being active and exercising as you have been doing so far.

Musculoskeletal: Reports bilateral knee pain.

Left knee pain.

She fell and thinks she twisted her knee in some kind of funky way. She reports that she has been limping ever since and it has not gotten better. She had a history of ulcer and is currently taking Tylenol for pain.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: Ulcer.

SOCIAL HISTORY

Patient reports that she is running with her niece.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports left knee pain.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neurological: Normal sensation in the bilateral upper and lower extremities.
Musculoskeletal: Examination of the left knee reveals edema, effusion, and mild range of motion. There is pain on palpation over the medial aspect of the knee. Negative Lachman's test, negative valgus test, and negative varus test.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS
X-rays of the left knee were obtained today and are not yet reviewed.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Angela Powell is an 81-year-old female who presents to the clinic today for evaluation of left knee pain.
Medical Reasoning:
- X-rays were obtained today but have not yet been reviewed.
- The patient reports that she had a history of ulcer and is currently taking Tylenol for pain.
- She has been limping ever since and it has not gotten better.
- Examination reveals edema, effusion, mild range of motion, pain on palpation over the medial aspect of the knee, negative Lachman's test, negative valgus test, and negative varus test.
Medical Treatment:
- I have discussed with the patient today that I do not think anything is torn in her knee based on examination findings. We did obtain x-rays today which were normal with no fractures or bony abnormalities noted.
- I have prescribed tramadol 50 mg twice daily for pain management as well as Tylenol as needed for breakthrough pain due to her history with ibuprofen use.
- I have recommended that she wear a knee immobilizer for 1 week to keep her from moving her left leg so that it can heal a little bit and reduce some inflammation that we are seeing here today. We will also ice it 3 or 4 times per day for 20 minutes at a time to help reduce swelling as well as mobilize it once we get home from here today. We will follow up in 2 weeks to reassess at which point we can discontinue icing if there is no improvement in symptoms at that time.
Patient Agreements:
The patient understands and agrees with all recommended medical treatment.

Diane Baker is a 28-year-old female with a past medical history significant for depression and hypertension who presents for emergency room follow-up. She reports that she was seen in the emergency room yesterday due to elevated blood pressure. She states that she was out walking in the sun and felt light-headed, and then started to fall. She was able to catch herself with her boyfriend. She notes that her blood pressure was elevated in the emergency room, almost. She also reports that she has been experiencing headaches.

She notes that her blood pressures have been running high once a week or once a month, and this usually occurs when she is traveling for work and not eating as well. She does not take her blood pressures when traveling.

Regarding her depression, she has been seeing a therapist once a week since last year and notes that this has helped. Her support system includes her boyfriend, mom, and brother who are all close to her.

Cardiovascular: Reports lightheadedness.
Neurological: Reports headache.

High blood pressure.

Depression.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient is doing well with therapy once weekly since last year, but we discussed that she may want to contact me if she needs anything further regarding this issue.
- Patient Education: We discussed the importance of continuing with therapy as needed for additional support.
- Medical Treatment: No medical treatment recommended at this time.

note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Follow-up for diabetes mellitus type 2, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, peripheral vascular disease with neuropathy.
Medical Reasoning:
The patient’s A1C was 9.9% last time we saw her. We discussed this with her at length and recommended increasing her glimepiride from 2 mg twice daily to 4 mg twice daily as this will help lower her A1C further. We also discussed the importance of eating healthier as well as drinking less soda and pasta since these are high in carbohydrates and sugars which can cause blood sugar spikes. The patient understands this recommendation and agrees to increase her glimepiride from 2 mg twice daily to 4 mg twice daily starting today with the new prescription that I will write for her today which will be for four milligrams twice a day. We also discussed how smoking cessation is important for all patients with diabetes mellitus type 2 as it can help improve glycemic control as well as reduce cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension and hyperlipidemia which can all contribute to peripheral vascular disease with neuropathy in this patient’s case.
Medical Treatment:
The patient will continue taking metformin by mouth two tablets by oral route two times per day as prescribed by me today. Her lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide will remain unchanged at one tablet once daily as prescribed by me today. Her metoprolol will remain unchanged at one tablet once daily as prescribed by me today. Her amlodipine will remain unchanged at one tablet once daily as prescribed by me today. Her atorvastatin will remain unchanged at one tablet once daily as prescribed by me today.
The patient’s blood pressure was checked again this morning and it was elevated at home (140/60). We discussed this with her again today and we agreed that we should recheck kidney function today since we have seen an improvement in blood pressure numbers since our last visit together.
The patient’s cholesterol levels were checked last time we saw her; they were high so we discussed continuing the high dose of Lipitor (atorvastatin) which she is already on since it protects the arteries from damage caused by cholesterol buildup which can lead to peripheral vascular disease with neuropathy in this patient’s case.
The patient continues to smoke despite our previous discussions regarding smoking cessation; however, I understand that quitting smoking is difficult for many patients so I have advised her that we will leave everything else the same until she decides she wants to quit smoking again.

Evaluation of numbness and tingling.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Elijah Cook is a 60-year-old right-handed male who presents today for evaluation of numbness and tingling. The onset of his symptoms began a few weeks ago, and he has been wearing a splint on his right wrist to help with the pain. He states that the numbness and tingling are worse on his right side, but both sides have gotten worse over the last month. He also reports mild stiffness in his neck, which he attributes to a contusion from the motor vehicle accident in December 2019.

The patient reports that the numbness and tingling are located on this side, from here to here up to about here. On the left side, they extend from the pinky and ring finger. The patient describes that they feel sore, sometimes throbbing, but overall weaker when using them. The tingling happens more when they hurt, but when it goes away, it is dull.

The patient denies any loss of sensation in his hands or fingers.

He has been taking Coreg for hypertension and Lexapro for anxiety. He had prediabetes but got it under control by changing his diet.

The patient denies any history of thyroid issues.
note.objective_exam:

note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Today's examination revealed bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome or potentially bilateral cubital tunnel syndrome. However, his symptom presentation suggests bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome as the nerve in his wrists are aggravated by past trauma.

After these studies are complete, he can return for a follow-up visit if he is still having symptoms at that time. If he continues to have symptoms after these studies we can consider a referral to our hand clinic possibly for injections or carpal tunnel release surgery. We could also refer him to an orthopedist for similar treatment options.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Follow-up of hospitalization.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Michelle King is a 39-year-old female who presents today for follow-up of her hospitalization. She was admitted to district regional hospital on 06/29/2021, and was discharged on 07/02/2021. The patient is a 39-year-old female with history of quadriplegia due to prior spinal cord injury. She was experiencing increasing concerns for spasms and lightheadedness, significant constipation, and reported diaphoresis. She was evaluated in the emergency department where she was febrile and had significantly elevated white blood cell count of 23,000. There were concerns for ongoing urinary tract infection, but she was treated with IV antibiotic therapy. She had labile blood pressure, headache, and vomiting. In the end, she slowly improved.

The patient reports that she went in to the ER because her blood pressure was out of control; it gave her a headache and made her throw up. At that time she felt much better after treatment.

She does have a supra-pubic catheter which has been reviewed by cultures.

The patient denies any pain or discomfort anywhere today.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Fever.
• Cardiovascular: Hypertension.
• Gastrointestinal: Constipation.
• Neurological: Dysreflexia.

note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN 
Acute to chronic constipation 
The patient presents today for follow-up regarding acute constipation secondary to dysreflexia from her quadriplegia status due to prior spinal cord injury. Her symptoms have resolved since discharge from the hospital after treatment with antibiotics for presumed UTI as well as IV hydration and bowel management with Miralax as needed as well as lactulose when severe constipation occurs. We discussed this further today in detail during our conversation today where we discussed that while dysreflexia can cause leukocytosis it typically does not cause elevated white blood cell counts without other signs of infection such as fever or purulent drainage from an infected site such as an indwelling catheter or wound site etc., however we did review cultures obtained from her supra-pubic catheter which were negative at this time so we do not believe there is an underlying UTI at this time but rather likely just elevated leukocytosis secondary to dysreflexia given her history of chronic constipation which can also cause elevation in white blood cells due to inflammation associated with chronic constipation issues such as diverticulitis etc., We discussed this further during our conversation today where I recommended that we wait a couple weeks before rechecking labs including CBCs again just to make sure there are no signs of worsening leukocytosis secondary to worsening constipation issues at this point given how well she has responded clinically since discharge from the hospital last week so I recommended that we wait until then before rechecking labs again if needed at that point if they remain elevated then we will need further evaluation for possible bowel pathology however if they normalize then I do not think there is anything else going on here at this point given how well she has responded clinically since discharge last week so I recommended continued conservative medical management including Miralax daily along with lactulose when severe constipation occurs along with increased fluid intake and dietary fiber supplementation until next visit in two weeks when we will repeat fasting labs including CBCs again just Acne.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Matthew Rogers is a 14-year-old male who presents today for an acne follow-up. At his last visit on 3/3/21, he was prescribed clindamycin lotion, tretinoin cream, and 4-5% benzoyl peroxide wash for face and 5-10% benzoyl peroxide wash for chest and back. He has been using the benzoyl peroxide twice daily, tretinoin cream at night, and clindamycin lotion every morning. He reports no redness, peeling, dryness or irritation with the use of these medications. He has not used the higher strength benzoyl peroxide wash on his chest and back as he has not had much of a flare there. He does report that his acne on his face is improving.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Skin: Reports improvement in acne.
Ears, Nose, Mouth: Denies any nasal congestion or rhinorrhea.
Eyes: Denies any eye irritation or discharge.
Ears: Denies any ear pain or discharge.
Respiratory: Denies any cough or shortness of breath.
note.objective_exam:

Skin Examination:
Scattered inflammatory papules and pustules across the upper back and posterior shoulders. Less than 5 inflammatory papules on the forehead, cheeks, and chin.
note.assessment_and_plan:

Acne.

6 weeks status post right medial unicompartmental arthroplasty.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Stephanie Morales is a 44-year-old female that presents today 6 weeks status post right medial unicompartmental arthroplasty. She reports that her right knee is doing well and she has no pain. She notes that she still has numbness in the area of the incision. She is concerned about returning to work as she is unable to go up and down steps with her current position.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports numbness in the area of the incision.
Neurological: Denies numbness.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Gait: Antalgic with a slight limp and decreased velocity.
Strength: 5/5 in all muscle groups.
Musculoskeletal: Examination of the right knee reveals a healed surgical scar, mild swelling, tenderness over the area of the incision. Range of motion is 0 to 120 degrees. Otherwise, examination of the right knee is normal.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-rays were reviewed today and show implants in stable position. No evidence of loosening or early complications.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

6 weeks status post right medial unicompartmental arthroplasty.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient's gait was antalgic with a slight limp and decreased velocity. Her range of motion was limited to 0 to 120 degrees due to pain from her surgical scar. Her strength was 5/5 in all muscle groups.
- Patient Education and Counseling: I advised her that it will take approximately two to three months before she feels like herself again after surgery. I also advised her that she should continue physical therapy to work on strength, range of motion, and endurance.
- Medical Treatment Plan: We discussed her employment situation today. She will need to wait another six weeks before returning to work as she cannot lift greater than five or ten pounds, stand for longer than half an hour, or sit for longer than half an hour at a time due to her current position at UPS. We discussed driving today as well. Normal reflex time has returned at six weeks post-op, but we discussed that return-to-driving is determined by when she feels safe driving again.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Abdominal pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Ashley James is a 14-year-old female who presents today for evaluation of abnormal renal ultrasound with an atrophic right kidney. She reports that she has been experiencing some stomach burning. She also endorses hesitancy while urinating and occasional dysuria. She denies hematuria. Some beverages are associated with dysuria, thus the patient drinks mainly water, Gatorade and V8 juice.

The patient plays on softball team and is interested in joining a drill team over the summer.

She has a history of end-stage chronic kidney disease that was dialysis dependent. Failed renal transplant.

PATIENT HISTORY

The patient is currently taking Pepcid 40 mg once daily and Claritin as needed for allergies.

FAMILY HISTORY

Paternal Grandfather: Deceased approximately 47 years old. Myocardial Infarction. Posterior Urethral Valves. Obstructive Neuropathy. End Stage Chronic Kidney Disease was Dialysis dependent. Failed Renal Transplant.
Paternal Great Aunt: End Stage Chronic Kidney Disease is Dialysis dependent. Type II Diabetes. Hypertension.
No family history of polycystic kidney disease.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Cardiovascular: Lungs and heart sound great.
Gastrointestinal: Well-appearing female, alert and oriented, sitting comfortably on my chair today, no acute distress noted otherwise with normal exam.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Abdominal ultrasound, 03/22/2021.
CT abdomen and pelvis, 03/22/2021.
CMP, 03/22/2021.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Ashley James is a 14-year-old female who presents today for evaluation of abnormal renal ultrasound with an atrophic right kidney.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient's abdominal pain may be related to her atrophic right kidney which is causing her left kidney to work harder than it should be doing so which could explain her hesitancy while urinating and occasional dysuria as well as her burning sensation when she drinks certain beverages like soda or Gatorade or V8 juice.
- Medical Treatment: We discussed the importance of avoiding non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicines like ibuprofen in favor of Tylenol due to their potential to cause further kidney damage in patients with pre-existing renal disease such as Ashley's. We also discussed the importance of staying well-hydrated during physical activity such as softball or drill team in order to avoid dehydration which can put tremendous strain on the kidneys. We recommended that we continue to monitor her blood pressure annually due to her increased risk for hypertension secondary to chronic kidney disease as well as proteinuria which can occur when kidneys do not work properly leading to protein in the urine. We recommended that we perform an annual ultrasound to monitor the size of her kidneys and their overall function as well as complete a urinalysis to continue to make sure that protein and blood are not in her urine every year going forward as well as perform a blood pressure check annually going forward.
- Patient Education: I recommended that Ashley continue eating a healthy diet and maintain an active lifestyle in order to keep both herself and her kidneys healthy throughout adulthood.

Sean Phillips is a 35-year-old male who presents today for the evaluation of left back pain. The onset of his symptoms began approximately 1 year ago after undergoing lumbar microdiscectomy in November 2020. He reports that he has had left-sided low back pain since then. He states that he has had lower extremity nerve pain as well. He was highly dosed up on gabapentin prior to surgery, which was difficult to withdraw from. He states that stretching helps with his symptoms, but bending over worsens them. He denies any physical activities that make his symptoms worse.

Musculoskeletal: Reports left-sided low back pain.
Neurological: Reports lower extremity nerve pain.

note.objective_results:

X-ray images of the lumbar spine reveal no evidence of fracture or other abnormalities in the spine or vertebrae. Previous surgical site is visible and appears to have healed properly.
note.assessment_and_plan:

Sean Phillips is a 35-year-old male who presents today for the evaluation of left-sided low back pain.

Medical Reasoning:
- X-rays were reviewed and revealed no evidence of fracture or other abnormalities in the spine or vertebrae. Previous surgical site is visible and appears to have healed properly.
- The patient reports history of status post lumbar microdiscectomy performed in 11/2020. Prior to microdiscectomy in 2020, he was taking high-dose gabapentin for severe nerve pain through his back and lower extremities.
- The patient reports history of muscle pull from having a misalignment in his spine.
- Medical Reasoning: I believe this is a muscle strain from having a misalignment in his spine.
Medical Treatment:
- Prescribe physical therapy for him at VA medical center today due to great results with previous physical therapy visits.
- Prescribe meloxicam instead of ibuprofen due to high dose ibuprofen use previously and discuss alternative options with him at pain management clinic today.
- Prescribe demerol today due to high dose ibuprofen use previously and discuss alternative options with him at pain management clinic today.

Right ankle pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Jacqueline Price is a 28-year-old female who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of right ankle pain. The onset of her symptoms began 3 days ago when she was doing something she did not want to be doing and fell off her bike. She reports that her ankle twisted outward at the time of the fall. She denies any numbness or tingling in her toes. She has been taking Tylenol for pain, but it has not helped. She heard a crack when she fell. She denies hearing anything pop at the time of injury.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: Reports taking Tylenol.

SOCIAL HISTORY

Patient reports that she has been mountain biking for 3 years.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports right ankle pain.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

VITALS: Temperature: 98.6; Blood Pressure: 118/77; Heart Rate: 77 bpm.
MSK: Examination of the right ankle reveals edema and erythema on the lateral malleolus on the right hand side, associated ecchymosis, and a few excoriations. There is pain to palpation of the right lateral malleolus. There is decreased flexion and extension of the right ankle as well as internal and external rotation. There is no apparent injury to the knee or foot.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS
X-ray of the right foot was obtained today and reviewed by me today, which shows no acute fracture or bony abnormality.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
For your assessment and plan I do believe you have an acute right ankle sprain. We will go ahead and put you in an air cast, we can give you some crutches, we will prescribe meloxicam fifteen milligrams once a day, you should ice the area for about twenty minutes five times a day, weight bear as tolerated. I am anticipating you to start feeling better in the next couple of weeks if you are not please come back here and see me and we will consider physical therapy or pursuing further imaging.

Musculoskeletal: Endorses right wrist soreness.

Neck: No jugular venous distention.

note.objective_results:

Mild mitral regurgitation was also noted on echocardiogram which is just a little floppy valve which is fine to monitor at this time.
- The patient endorses soreness in his right wrist post cardiac catheterization, but this has improved.
- The patient denies shortness of breath with ambulation or movement.
- His blood pressure today was 127/60 which is good for him given his history of hypertension.
- His ejection fraction was approximately 50% on echocardiogram which is low normal but not bad so that's good so okay just i would just watch your salt intake okay.
- The patient reports that he enjoys swimming and he misses swimming so we discussed this today and I recommended that we start him back up with swimming once again, however I advised him to do a few laps at first until we see how he tolerates it then we can increase his activity level as tolerated. We also discussed ordering some liver function studies and lipid panel to follow up with next time we meet.

The patient is a 33-year-old female who presents today for evaluation of right knee pain.

Medical Reasoning:
- X-rays were obtained today and reviewed in office today. They appear normal with no obvious signs of fracture or dislocation.
- I am suspicious for a posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) sprain given her history and exam findings.
- MRI scan may be indicated to evaluate for other potential soft tissue injuries such as meniscal tears or chondral lesions.

- Patient Agreements:
- The patient understands and agrees with recommended medical treatment plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Right elbow pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Zachary Wood is a 45-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of right elbow pain. The onset of his pain began yesterday. He denies any trauma to the area. He reports that he was up and moving around as usual yesterday, but denies doing anything unusual. He has been taking Motrin for the pain, but it has not helped.

The patient reports that his pain is localized to his left arm from the elbow up to the neck. He describes it as achiness, heaviness, and numbness. The patient denies any chest pain or shortness of breath.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: Hypertension, Type 2 Diabetes.

CURRENT MEDICATIONS

Metformin 500 mg; Norvasc 2.5 mg.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neurological: Examination of the extremities reveals decreased sensation in the left upper extremity from the elbow to the neck. Otherwise normal examination.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Hematology: Hemoglobin A1c was 7.2.
Cardiology: EKG revealed a grade 1 systolic murmur.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Zachary Wood is a 45-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of right elbow pain.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient's symptoms are concerning for musculoskeletal pain secondary to sleeping on his arm wrong or overuse injury, however, given his history of hypertension and diabetes, we also need to rule out cardiac etiology.
- Medical Treatment: We will obtain an EKG today to evaluate for possible cardiac etiology. We will also obtain a glucose test today to evaluate for diabetes mellitus type II and adjust his current medications accordingly if needed. We will prescribe aspirin and nitroglycerin for chest pain relief today as well.
- Patient Education and Counseling: I have counseled him on the importance of managing his blood pressure and diabetes through diet and exercise.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Abdominal pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Karen Allen is a 34-year-old female who presents today with abdominal pain. The onset of her abdominal pain began approximately 10 days ago with mild discomfort in the right side. She notes that the pain has been worsening over the last couple of days. She rates her pain as a 4-7 on a scale of 0-10 today. She notes that her pain is usually worse after meals and better in the morning before she eats. She denies any radiation of her pain to other areas. She has had some nausea and heartburn but no vomiting. She denies any urinary symptoms or changes in bowel habits.

She reports that she is not as hungry since she has been nauseated and feels fatigued over the last week.

She denies any travel outside of Wisconsin recently.

The patient reports that she has had chronic migraines for many years and responds well to excedrin migraine when needed. She also uses sumatriptan occasionally for breakthrough migraines or worse migraines.

She reports that she has been taking lisinopril 20 mg per day for hypertension, which she states she checks daily at home, but notes that her blood pressure is elevated today.
note.objective_exam:

Cardiovascular: Grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur heard, unchanged from prior exam, just means i hear some heart sounds as i'm listening to your heart there i'm not too concerned about that we'll watch that otherwise normal cardiovascular exam.

Gastrointestinal: Tenderness in right upper quadrant, mild to moderate tenderness, equivocal Murphy's sign.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Abdominal Pain: Acute abdominal pain with right upper quadrant tenderness. I am concerned for possible gallstones or possibly even an infection in the gallbladder. We will order a CBC, chem-12, urinalysis, pregnancy test and right upper quadrant ultrasound today.
Migraines: Chronic migraines with occasional bouts of migraines recently. Continue excedrin as needed over-the-counter for treatment there and also sumatriptan as needed for breakthrough migraine pain.
Hypertension: Adequate control with lisinopril 20 mg per day daily at home; we will continue lisinopril 20 mg per day daily at home and write you a refill prescription for it today.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Hacking cough.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Hannah Wilson is a 41-year-old female who presents today for the evaluation of a hacking cough. She reports that the onset of her cough began 3 days ago when she was around her sister who has been sick with similar symptoms. She has been drinking lots of water and taking over-the-counter cough medication, but this has not helped. She denies fever, shortness of breath, body aches, nausea or vomiting.

She reports that she has had seasonal allergies around spring time and denies any nasal congestion or sore throat. She also denies any history of diarrhea.

The patient reports that her blood pressure has been elevated at home and she is currently taking hydrochlorothiazide daily. She notes that she has been trying to stay away from salty foods but has had trouble with sugar intake.

PAST HISTORY

Medical: Type 2 diabetes.
Allergies: Seasonal allergies.
Medications: Metformin 500 mg; Hydrochlorothiazide.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Constitutional: Denies fever, weight loss, weight gain.
Respiratory: Reports hacking cough, sore throat, nasal congestion.
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain or dyspnea on exertion.
Gastrointestinal: Denies nausea or vomiting.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Head and Neck:
- Ears, Nose, Mouth and Throat: Erythema of the pharynx. No exudates noted on tonsils. Bilateral maxillary sinus tenderness. No frontal sinus tenderness noted.
- Neck: Anterior cervical adenopathy.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Upper respiratory infection.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient presents today for evaluation of a hacking cough which started 3 days ago when she was around her sister who also had similar symptoms. She denies fever, shortness of breath, body aches, nausea or vomiting. Her blood pressure is elevated at home and she is currently taking hydrochlorothiazide daily which she states she tolerates well without any side effects. Her blood work at her last visit was normal with no evidence of diabetes mellitus type II at this time.
- Patient Education and Counseling: I discussed with the patient the importance of resting and staying hydrated to help with her symptoms as well as the importance of avoiding salty foods due to her hypertension as well as sugar intake due to her diabetes mellitus type II. We discussed that it may be difficult for her to avoid sugar intake due to being around family members who have been sick recently but we discussed ways in which we can work together to help manage this including checking for COVID-19 today if she is willing to do so today as well as continuing to check her blood pressure at home several times per week in order to monitor how well it is controlled while continuing to take hydrochlorothiazide daily in the morning in order to avoid increased urination which can occur with this medication due to its diuretic properties.
- Medical Treatment Plan: Continue Metformin 500 mg twice daily as prescribed for diabetes mellitus type II. Continue hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once daily in the morning in order to help control blood pressure while avoiding increased urination which can occur with this medication due to its diuretic properties. Continue over-the-counter cough medication as needed for symptom relief while avoiding Coricidin HBP due to its potential side effects on blood pressure control if taken concurrently with other medications such as metformin which can cause hypoglycemia if not properly monitored by a physician's office or hospital setting.
- Additional Testing Recommended Today: We will check you for COVID-19 today if you are willing.

note.subjective:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Left shoulder pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Betty Rogers is a 50-year-old female who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of left shoulder pain. The onset of her symptoms began 3 weeks ago and she denies any associated trauma. She is very active and has been renovating her basement recently. She denies any previous history of left shoulder pain. She reports that she has been taking Tylenol Extra Strength, 2 tablets every 6 to 8 hours, which does help take the edge off her pain.

She reports that she is unable to move her left arm for me. She states that anytime she tries to reach for something or lift anything, she has a lot of pain and does not even try to raise her arm over her head because that is too painful. Her pain is constant and if there is any pressure, such as when she tries to sleep at night, she cannot even lay on her left side because it gives her a hard time due to the pain being always present. She states that when she sleeps directly on it, the pain goes up.

She denies numbness or tingling in her arm or hand.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports left shoulder pain.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neurological: Neurovascular exam of the left arm reveals brisk cap refill in less than 3 seconds bilaterally. Motor and sensation are intact to light touch bilaterally.
Musculoskeletal: Examination of the left shoulder reveals limited active and passive range of motion. Tenderness over greater tuberosity of the humerus. No tenderness at sternoclavicular or clavicular joints.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-ray imaging of the left shoulder was obtained today and reviewed in office today. There are no signs of fracture or bony abnormality.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Betty Rogers is a 50-year-old female who presents today for evaluation of left shoulder pain.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient's symptoms are most likely due to rotator cuff tendinopathy.
- Medical Treatment Plan: I have reviewed your x-ray results with you today and there are no signs of fracture or bony abnormality so we will order an MRI of your shoulder just to make sure nothing else is going on with your left shoulder today. I have also referred you for physical therapy for approximately 6-8 weeks as well as prescribed Tylenol p.r.n., if your symptoms do not improve we can then consider maybe like a steroid injection into your left shoulder which could hopefully get you some relief.
Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with my recommended medical treatment plan.

Right knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Matthew Allen is a 40-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of right knee pain. The onset of his right knee pain began yesterday when he was playing basketball and he felt like his knee popped. He states that he has not played basketball in 2 years. He denies any history of trauma to the right knee. He reports that the pain is localized to the medial aspect of his right knee and is described as achy. The patient states that he can bear weight on his right leg, but favors it. He denies any numbness or tingling in the right leg. The patient reports that since he slept overnight, the swelling has decreased some.

The patient reports taking Norvasc 5 mg daily and Metformin 500 mg daily. He states that he has been taking Tylenol for pain management.

The patient denies any history of hypertension or diabetes.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports right knee pain.
Cardiovascular: Reports hypertension.
Endocrine: Reports diabetes.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Constitutional: Well-nourished male in no apparent distress.
Respiratory: Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Cardiovascular: Grade 2 systolic ejection murmur heard at the left lower sternal border, otherwise normal examination of the heart.
Neurological: No evidence of sensory or motor deficits in the lower extremities.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

X-ray of Matthew Allen's right knee was reviewed today and revealed no fractures or bony abnormalities.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Right knee strain, MCL strain.
- Medical Reasoning: Matthew Allen sustained a medial collateral ligament strain when playing basketball yesterday. His exam today revealed tenderness over the medial aspect of his right knee with edema and ecchymosis present as well as positive varus and valgus testing. An MRI was recommended to further evaluate for ligamentous injury.
- Medical Treatment Plan: Continue Tylenol for pain management until we obtain an MRI to evaluate for ligamentous injury. CHIEF COMPLAINT

Elevated and fluctuating blood pressure.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Robert Harris is a 67-year-old male with a history of essential hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis who is here today with elevated and fluctuating blood pressures. He reports that his blood pressure has been well controlled over the last 3 to 4 weeks. However, he has experienced periods where he felt lightheaded and had a slight headache. When he checked his blood pressure, the upper number was occasionally over 180 mm Hg, which is higher than any of the numbers have been in the past.

The patient denies passing out or chest pain. He does report some heaviness in his chest when his blood pressure is elevated. He also reports occasional dizziness and a slight headache when his blood pressure is elevated. The patient denies any numbness or weakness, balance instability, fever, nausea or vomiting, diarrhea, palpitations or heart racing.

SOCIAL HISTORY

The patient enjoys playing golf.

MEDICATIONS

He continues to take lisinopril 20 mg twice per day; atorvastatin; occasional Tylenol.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Cardiovascular: Grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur unchanged from prior exam. Otherwise unremarkable.
Respiratory: Mild bilateral bibasilar rales otherwise unremarkable air movement.
Musculoskeletal: Trace lower extremity edema bilaterally.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Elevated Blood Pressure.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient's blood pressure has been well controlled over the last 3 to 4 weeks but has been elevated at times. His symptoms include lightheadedness and headaches when his blood pressure is elevated.
- Medical Treatment: I have increased lisinopril to 60 mg twice daily and added hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily to help even things out. We will follow up in 2 weeks to assess how he is doing with these changes.
- Patient Education: I advised him that it's important for him to check his blood pressure twice daily for the next 2 weeks while we monitor how he responds to these changes.
Hyperlipidemia.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient's cholesterol levels are still high despite taking atorvastatin. We will order additional labs including a cholesterol panel, CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel and urinalysis as well as review his current management plan for hyperlipidemia.
- Medical Treatment: We will continue the current management plan with atorvastatin until we review additional labs in 2 weeks.
Osteoarthritis of the knees.
- Medical Reasoning: The patient continues to experience pain while golfing but otherwise tolerates activity well without any limitations other than weather changes that may limit his ability to play golf occasionally. He reports taking Tylenol for mild pain as needed but does not require opioids for pain control at this time.
- Medical Treatment: Continue current management plan with Tylenol for mild pain as needed while continuing to stay active as best he can without overdoing it and golfing when possible.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Headache.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Donna Allen is a 37-year-old female who presents today with complaints of headache. She has a history of hypertension and diabetes. The onset of her headaches began about 3 weeks ago and have been progressively worsening. She has noticed that her blood pressure has been running high, and she has been taking lisinopril 20 mg once a day but has been forgetting to take it on the weekends when she is most busy. She denies taking anything for her headaches, but does take Tylenol occasionally. She rates her headache at 7/10 when it first starts, but after taking Tylenol it goes down to 4/10. She denies any nasal congestion or runny nose.

She reports that she has had migraines in the past, but not like this one. She denies any coughing or sneezing.

She notes that she gets her allergies in the springtime, but this year they are different than usual.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Head: Reports headaches.
• Cardiovascular: Reports hypertension.
• Neurological: Reports headaches.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neurological: Tenderness over frontal sinuses bilaterally and tenderness over the right cheekbone.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Donna Allen is a 37-year-old female who presents today with complaints of headache.

Medical Reasoning:
- The patient's headache began about 3 weeks ago and have been progressively worsening. Her blood pressure has also been running high since then, which may be related to her headaches.
- Her headaches are likely due to increased sympathetic activity secondary to hypertension as well as possibly secondary to diabetes mellitus.
- The patient's blood pressure was normal last time we saw her, so increasing lisinopril from 20 mg once a day to 40 mg once a day should help control her hypertension and hopefully decrease her headache frequency and severity.
- We will order some normal blood work including hemoglobin A1c as well as laboratory tests to evaluate for diabetes mellitus.
- We will also provide diabetic education for Donna today so that she can better manage her diabetes at home.
- I recommended that Donna continue walking as exercise is wonderful for everything going on today.

Vision changes.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Matthew Thomas is a pleasant 65-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of vision changes. The patient reports that he has been having trouble adjusting in the dark, especially when eating out at fancy restaurants. He also reports that when looking at straight lines, such as door frames, they look crooked to him. The patient denies any visual loss in his left eye. He denies any diplopia or double vision.

The patient reports that he has been smoking 1 pack of cigarettes daily for the past and has tried hypnosis, lozenges, and chewing gum to help him quit smoking but has not been successful.

The patient reports that he has a history of high blood pressure and is currently taking his blood pressure medication as prescribed. He states that he has not taken his medication for a while and it is back in the cupboard.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Eyes: Decreased vision when reading especially in dim environments.
• Neurological: No diplopia or double vision.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Eyes: Anterior segment examination reveals posterior chamber intraocular lenses in both eyes. The cornea is clear with no neovascularization or cup-to-disc ratio of 2. Fundus examination of the right eye shows the retina to be attached 360 degrees without holes or tears noted. RPE changes are present in the fovea. Posterior segment examination shows drusen under the RPE which is consistent with age-related macular degeneration (AMD). There is also presence of subretinal fluid and exudate accumulation which is positive for hemorrhage. Fluorescein angiography reveals focal leakage in the right eye consistent with wet AMD.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

OCT exam shows drusen deposits under the RPE which is consistent with AMD. Subretinal fluid and choroidal neovascular membrane can also be visualized on this test.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Matthew Thomas is a pleasant 65-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of vision changes.

The diagnostic test and eye exams are consistent with wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD) which is advanced to a stage that usually leads to more severe vision loss.
This happens when abnormal blood vessels start to grow beneath the retina, which then leak fluid and blood, creating a large blind spot in the center of your visual field.
It is the most common cause of severe vision loss.
We have a plan for him today once a month we will give him an injection of Lucentis into his vitreous portion of his eye after we numb his eye so he will not feel any pain at all. Patients report no pain at all for this injection at all.
The injections given over time can slow down the rate of vision decline and maybe even stop it however there could be a situation where you may still note a small amount of vision loss but this is your best chance of maintaining that vision for as long as you can.
I have given him a lot of information today and I want to pause here before we get him scheduled for that injection today to see if he has any questions or concerns before we get him scheduled.

The patient reports that he has been having trouble adjusting in the dark, especially when eating out at fancy restaurants. He also reports that when looking at straight lines, such as door frames, they look crooked to him. The patient denies any visual loss in his left eye. He denies any diplopia or double vision.

The patient reports that he has been smoking 1 pack of cigarettes daily for the past and has tried hypnosis, lozenges, and chewing gum to help him quit smoking but has not been successful.

The patient reports that he has a history of high blood pressure and is currently taking his blood pressure medication as prescribed. He states that he has not taken his medication for a while and it is back in the cupboard.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Eyes: Decreased vision when reading especially in dim environments.
• Neurological: No diplopia or double vision.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Eyes: Anterior segment examination reveals posterior chamber intraocular lenses in both eyes. The cornea is clear with no neovascularization or cup-to-disc ratio of 2. Fundus examination of the right eye shows the retina to be attached 360 degrees without holes or tears noted. RPE changes are present in the fovea. Posterior segment examination shows drusen under the RPE which is consistent with age-related macular degeneration (AMD). There is also presence of subretinal fluid and exudate accumulation which is positive for hemorrhage. Fluorescein angiography reveals focal leakage in the right eye consistent with wet AMD.

RESULTS

OCT exam shows drusen deposits under the RPE which is consistent with AMD. Subretinal fluid and choroidal neovascular membrane can also be visualized on this test.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Matthew Thomas is a pleasant 65-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of vision changes.

The diagnostic test and eye exams are consistent with wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD) which is advanced to a stage that usually leads to more severe vision loss.
This happens when abnormal blood vessels start to grow beneath the retina, which then leak fluid and blood, creating a large blind spot in the center of your visual field.
It is the most common cause of severe vision loss.
We have a plan for him today once a month we will give him an injection of Lucentis into his vitreous portion of his eye after we numb his eye so he will not feel any pain at all. Patients report no pain at all for this injection at all.
The injections given over time can slow down the rate of vision decline and maybe even stop it however there could be a situation where you may still note a small amount of vision loss but this is your best chance of maintaining that vision for as long as you can.
I have given him a lot of information today and I want to pause here before we get him scheduled for that injection today to see if he has any questions or concerns before we get him scheduled.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Follow-up of nonsmall cell lung cancer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Angela King is a 58-year-old female who presents today for follow-up of nonsmall cell lung cancer. She reports that she has been experiencing shortness of breath over the weekend. She had previously been very active, taking mile-long walks with her doberman. Her husband has been her support system and her daughter has also been helpful. She is currently taking cisplatin, etoposide, and Zofran.

The patient reports that she has been coughing but denies phlegm. She denies fever. She does report pain when swallowing, which she describes as a sharp pain in her chest when swallowing. She denies any body aches or sore throat.

On examination, there is erythema on the anterior aspect of the chest on the left side due to radiation therapy. There is no edema in the extremities.

The patient reports that she was nauseated and tired after her last dose of chemotherapy but took Zofran which helped with nausea and fatigue.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Denies fever.
• Respiratory: Reports shortness of breath, dry cough, dysphagia.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neck: No cervical lymphadenopathy or subclavicular adenopathy.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm without murmurs.
Respiratory: Crackles in bilateral lungs bilaterally.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

Pathology report shows evidence of a 4.4 cm left upper lobe nodule; chest x-ray obtained today not yet reviewed.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Nonsmall cell lung cancer.
• Medical Reasoning: The patient presents today for follow-up after being diagnosed with stage 3 nonsmall cell lung cancer. We are continuing her current chemotherapy regimen with cisplatin and etoposide as well as radiation therapy at 45 Gy in fractions to reduce tumor size prior to resectional surgery if possible.
• Medical Treatment Plan: We will continue her current chemotherapy regimen with cisplatin and etoposide as well as radiation therapy at 45 Gy in fractions to reduce tumor size prior to resectional surgery if possible. We will also prescribe prednisone 40 mg daily for five days to help reduce inflammation in the lungs and improve breathing.
Radiation pneumonitis.
• Medical Reasoning: The patient presents today for evaluation of radiation pneumonitis due to radiation therapy for nonsmall cell lung cancer. This is an expected finding due to radiation therapy for this patient’s diagnosis.
• Medical Treatment Plan: Prednisone 40 mg daily for five days will be prescribed to help reduce inflammation in the lungs and improve breathing while she continues radiation treatment.
Painful swallowing (odyophagia).
• Medical Reasoning: The patient presents today for evaluation of painful swallowing secondary to radiation pneumonitis due to radiation therapy for nonsmall cell lung cancer. This is an expected finding due to radiation pneumonitis from this patient’s diagnosis.
• Medical Treatment Plan: Lidocaine squishy swallows will be prescribed four times daily until resolution.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Kidney stone.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Joshua Reyes is a 18-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of a kidney stone. He reports that he has been experiencing right flank pain radiating to his groin for the last 2 weeks. The pain is intermittent and is under control, but he experiences bouts where it gets out of control. He denies any hematuria. He has had some chills but denies fevers. He has been taking ibuprofen for the pain, which helps somewhat, but the pain persists. His pain score is 4/10 when it gets out of control and 1-2/10 most of the time.

Mr. Reyes reports that he has had kidney stones in the past and that they usually pass within a week, although some have required surgical intervention or lithotripsy.

Mr. Reyes denies nausea or vomiting.

He reports that all family members have had kidney stones in the past.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Denies fever, chills, or weight loss.
• Musculoskeletal: Reports right flank pain radiating to groin.
note.objective_exam:
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

CVS: Tenderness to palpation over right costovertebral angle.
note.objective_results:
RESULTS

CT scan of the right flank was reviewed today, 05/06/2022. It revealed a kidney stone measuring 0.5 cm in size, located on the proximal right ureter. There is no evidence of hydronephrosis.
note.assessment_and_plan:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Joshua Reyes is a 18-year-old male who presents today for evaluation of a kidney stone.

Medical Reasoning:
- The patient presents with right flank pain radiating to his groin for the last 2 weeks and denies hematuria.
- His symptoms are consistent with a kidney stone.
- The CT scan revealed a kidney stone measuring 0.5 cm in size located on the proximal right ureter with no evidence of hydronephrosis.
- The patient has had previous episodes of passing stones independently and requires surgical intervention or lithotripsy occasionally.
- His current symptoms are mild and do not require surgical intervention at this time.
- We discussed treatment options including medical management with ibuprofen and tramadol as needed for breakthrough pain as well as further treatment options including lithotripsy if needed at this time.
- We discussed lifestyle modifications including increased fluid intake to help pass the stone today and in the future.
- We discussed additional testing including urinalysis and urine culture if needed based on results from these tests to rule out infection at this time.
- We discussed follow-up in 1-2 weeks if symptoms persist or if there is still evidence of a stone present at that time.

He notes that he has been watching his salt intake, but admits to having a few family gatherings over the holidays and believes this may have contributed to his current symptoms. He denies any weight loss or fever.

The patient reports that he has noticed swelling in his legs and urinates at least once at night, which is more than usual. His last visit with his nephrologist was about 1 month ago.

The patient denies chest pain or dyspnea on exertion. However, he does report waking up short of breath once before and does not currently experience this symptom.

Allergies: None reported.
Constitutional: History of coronary disease.
